He claims to be the biblical giant Og, King of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim, who survived the Flood by riding the ridgepole of Noah's Ark, holding an umbrella over a poorly-sealed hatch. On this account he is older than the Flood.

The Divine Commission

God has charged him with protecting Pilgrim even into hell, and he feels bound to honor the commission despite his own disbelief. He wears the Golden Shovel and the Pilgrim Staff and holds the titles of both Lord Temporal and Lord Spiritual. He works professionally as "the Umbrella," providing services in shielding and protection.

I don't believe in him, but I believe even less in myself without him. And I have a commission from beyond to guard him forever, and to share his destruction if I cannot avert it. I believe that I have this commission from beyond, but I do not believe in any beyond.

Noah Zontik

Paradoxical Relationship

Despite protecting the protagonist, Zontik/Scath is often his harshest critic. He accuses him of being "a derivative projection," warns him of danger, and challenges his philosophy. He belongs to the Dusmano cult but "struggles with its implications." He recognizes the evil but cannot abandon his charge.

Fate

In the final chapter, Og Scath acts as coroner at Polder's execution. He says: "I'm not very friendly to him anymore. . . it is written somewhere that I would go to hell for him, or with him." When Polder dies, Og Scath dies suddenly. Doctor Vonk explains, "He believed he had to go with Polder to shield him. He may have gone an instant early."

Cyrus Evenhand Rut (The Rod/Scepter) The Consul

"One Powerful Enemy" · Secret Ruler · The Good Man

Identity

Cyrus Evenhand is "accounted a good man," "serious, pleasant, powerful," and the holder of "the office like none other in the country," which requires complete anonymity. His code name "Rut" means rod, scepter, or authority in German. He is revealed to be the Consul, the secret ruler of the world where Pilgrim Dusmano operates.

He is described as "tall and slim" and "unpolished," without the protagonist's suavity. His strength comes from goodness and legitimate authority rather than charisma. He stands for the accountability, consequence, and moral order that the protagonist denies.

The Conflict

Evenhand and his eight henchmen are sworn to destroy the protagonist, recognizing him as a corrupter and murderer. The protagonist declares war by killing Hut: "my declaration of war? Killing Hut was my ante in the game." Evenhand's forces are overwhelmed. He and all eight henchmen are killed, and their fortunes are "knackered" (processed) by the protagonist's gilded statue.

It's easy enough to kill this Pilgrim Dusmano. . . The problem isn't that tall, Evenhand. You make mountains out of middens.

One of the Henchmen

The Eight Henchmen

Evenhand's eight associates have German-derived code names ending in “-ut.” They are wealthy and outwardly secure, but Pilgrim exploits their identities to expose them to violence. The knacker processes eight fortunes, including Evenhand's, while holding Wut's over for payment. The gold used for the Holy Knacker comes from the Mut cult's hoard.

Blut (Blood/Family)
One of the "minor" henchmen. Killed early by mobs who "tore Blut to pieces" before the protagonist's people could reach him. Pieces of his body are brought to the Media Lords. Pilgrim declares: "Blut was a minor one, but we will quickly come to the main."
Brut (Brood/Spawn)
One of Evenhand's associates. Killed along with the others; his fortune processed by the knacker. His name suggests generation and offspring.
Flut (Flood/Overflow)
One of Evenhand's associates, his code name meaning "the breaking-out" or "overflowing." Killed with the others; his body and fortune processed. A young Media Lord boasts: "We have nailed their hides to the barn door, as the ancient saying has it."
Glut (Blaze/Flame)
One of Evenhand's associates. His name suggests fire and burning, which may anticipate the furnaces in which the henchmen's gold is melted. Killed and processed with the others.
Gut (Property)
One of Evenhand's associates. His code name means property or goods. He is among the men unmasked by the Media Lords and targeted by the crowds; his estate is among those the knacker processes for Pilgrim.
Hut (Harbor/Shelter/Hat)
Hut is the first henchman Pilgrim kills directly. Pilgrim describes the murder as his declaration of war and his ante in the game with Evenhand. The code name carries associations of shelter and guardianship; the killing begins the open hostilities.
Mut (Courage/Holiness-through-Strength)
The powerful, bulky assailant who bleeds Pilgrim with a ritual knife. Publicly known as Satterfield, he heads the Strength-in-Purity and Strength-in-Serenity cults. His hoard exceeds twenty-six thousand kilograms of gold. Pilgrim first plans to gild Mut's corpse but makes the idol from the knacker instead. Wut's fortune is said to be slightly larger, though in a less delightful form.
Wut (Rage/Mania)
Described as "very, very rich," with a fortune "slightly greater than that of Mut." His code name means rage or mania. The knacker saves him for last, demanding full payment before processing "rich Wut." In the afterlife Narrow Corner sequence, Wut appears as "an intelligent, calculating, canny, relentless, unforgetting, unforgiving man" possessed by "rage and mania", which suggests that the code name describes his nature.

Hector Bogus

Hector Bogus

Media Lord · Brigadier of Police · "One Powerful Enemy" (Later)

A local Eidolon and Media Lord, technically adept at creating, animating, and torturing small effigies. Polder recognizes him as a counterpart of Trenchant. Bogus kills Polder with the modified Hand from Heaven, then revives him when Og intervenes. Pressured by Moira and Og, he provides cult publicity. At the final death-weighing he acts as brigadier of police and torments a sliver of Polder's heart.

His name suggests falseness and illusion. Bogus works in artificial realities, fake spectacles, and manufactured miracles, and he creates what others believe in.

The Morey Siblings

Mary Morey Maria del Mar

Cult Devotee · Furnace Operator · The Woman in Sunlight

The most devoted of the cult followers. She appears in the frame narrative as "Maria del Mar, a young and taut-faced girl" mourning at Pilger Tisman's burial. As Mary Morey, she is one of Pilgrim Dusmano's morning students, always found "in the sunlight" while her brother James lurks in shadows.

She operates the furnaces in the All-Effects Hall where the Holy Knacker is cast. She can "flute her tongue in odd ways to form the various shapes in smoke." She recognizes Pilgrim as "an Anti-Christus" but stays loyal. When the militia comes, she volunteers: "We're going with him. Don't let him get too far ahead of us or he'll go into panic."

After death she appears as the ARIEL servitor and continues to follow the protagonist.

James Morey Jacob del Mar Jake Mara

Cult Devotee · Shadow Dweller · The Hound

Mary's brother, always found "in the shadows" while she occupies the sunlight, which leads to speculation that "he is her shadow." Although he admits, "I don't understand old Dusmano at all," he stays a leading member of the cult.

He assists in cult operations: filling the crock to drown the statuette with Pilgrim's former eyes, operating the hoist and furnace during the Holy Knacker's creation. After the casting, James's gold lust and blood lust drain away, and he is left sobbing silently in the shadows.

After death he appears as the HOUND servitor in the Narrow Corner sequence and fights Wut and other enemies.

Moira Mara

Parallel Figure · Polder's Devotee

The Polder Dossman–world parallel to Mary Morey/Maria del Mar. Her name continues the M-alliteration pattern across incarnations. She serves Polder as Mary serves Pilgrim, as a devoted companion who recognizes his nature.

The Students

Rhinestone Suderman

Student · Cult Founder · Compelled Devotee

"A large, fair-haired young female person" and student of Pilgrim Dusmano. She proposes founding the cult: "Is anyone here interested in forming a Pilgrim Dusmano cult?" When challenged, she explains: "We’re compelled to. . . . By a compulsion, of course. By a blind compulsion. All cults are started by such compulsions."

She prophesies "the last sunny day ever in this world for us" and encourages the others to call Pilgrim "chaotic" rather than "mixed up": "This gives us more scope. In one of the mythologies, great things were brought out of chaos."

Howard Praise

Student · Reluctant Cultist

A student uncertain about joining: "I'm on the edge of joining his cult, but what if there is nothing in him at all?" He mumbles that Pilgrim is "a little unreal when he implies that the worlds are a little unreal." Despite his doubts, he joins and stays. When the militia demand Pilgrim's location, Howard declares flatly, "Nobody here will tell you."

The Professionals

Clarence Music

Curator · Daylight Museum · Cult Member

Curator of the Daylight Museum where Pilgrim spends mornings examining artifacts. He observes that Pilgrim "exteriorizes badly or unevenly. . . He is a pleasure seeker in all things, but for balance he pushes it too far. There's a lot of raw bloodiness associated with his pleasures." Despite this clinical assessment, he joins the cult and attends the final gathering.

Randal Muckman

Media Lord · Cult Member

A "Media Lord" who joins Pilgrim's cult. The Media Lords control eidetic reality: illusions, projections, and manufactured experiences. His membership shows Pilgrim's influence reaching into the institutions that shape public perception.

The Doctors

Judas Raffels

Doctor Medical · Cult Member · Betrayer

One of the "Doctors Medical" in Pilgrim's cult. When militia demand Pilgrim's location, Raffels betrays him: "Dusmano is out by that parkway. . . hiding in the largest thorn thicket there. Come. I'll show you." He whistles "Heads Will Roll" as he goes. He also attends Pilgrim's death to collect his stipend and feels that he has "attended Dusmano at his death at some earlier time."

John Augustine

Doctor Medical · Lord Spiritual

Another Doctor Medical and "Lord Spiritual" in the cult. He and Raffels position themselves to collect death-stipends: "We are two very good medical doctors. Why should we let lesser doctors receive stipends for pronouncing persons dead?" He accompanies Raffels to witness Pilgrim's execution.

Others

Spurgeon

Commerce Assistant

Works for Pilgrim "in his commerces." Takes a monthly inventory of trees in the parkway region, and his records show that Pilgrim's "cursed persimmon tree" never existed at all.

Lord Fairfronter

Media Lord · Cult Devotee

Wears the tiny Pilgrim Staff pin marking his cult membership. Fairfronter questions Pilgrim about his imminent departure and succession, and offers a polished appraisal of his posthuman personality. Noah Zontik, rather than Fairfronter, predicts that the Media Lords will destroy Pilgrim.

Cordcutter

Young Media Lord

Reports on the henchmen's deaths: "Blut has already been killed. . . The people got to him before we had hardly started on our instigation." Brings pieces of Blut's body to the Media Lords.

Trenchant (the Rubber Knife)

Spy · Challenger

A spy who challenges Pilgrim at the Media Club, arguing that he is destroying the world's foundations. When Pilgrim proclaims "I'm no whisper of evil. I'm a shouting of evil!" Trenchant is seized by young Media Lords, left "bloodily unmanned" with an eye dangling, and then dismembered by Pilgrim with his bare hands: "Swift, sure pleasure, vital and mortal." Wears a "Camel's Revenge" badge.

The Pym Family

Aubrey Pym

Employee · Messenger · Sacrifice

Works at Pilgrim's commodity terminal, asks for a raise, and is selected with his family as this week's "messengers" to Supply. The sending requires that the messengers be "apprehensive, nervous, determined, daring, creative in mind." Pilgrim grants him a doubled salary with fringes like the bangles on a carnival girl's jacket before ritually killing the entire family with a stone knife.

His wife Mrs. Pym recalls that the Hemsteds went to "Dongola" earlier that year. The younger Pym child defies Pilgrim: "You can cut my head clear off, but you can't kill me. . . I'll hide in the passages and in the glaciers, and I'll trap you there." This child takes "a lot of killing," and one hate-filled eye survives the people-grinder, "riding the remaining effluvium" and glaring at Pilgrim. The threat may be fulfilled in the Narrow Corner, where the child appears as a fire-drake.

Cannes World

Janie

Elite · Pelion's Couch Companion

A melodious-voiced elite on Cannes World, "frequent couch companion" of Pelion Tuscamondo. She first notices the scandal of the artificial Jezebel: "You are not using live persons! . . . That was a sham Jezebel they used!" Her vigilance triggers the Marshal's exposure and execution.

Albert Fineface

Captain of Elites · Factor

"Captain of the elites for that day" who interrogates the Marshal of Animations. He stabs the Marshal's tongue with a dagger to force speech, then orders the Marshal's daughter dismembered. He later acts as a broker of dubious transactions and offers Pelion entry into the Group Unconscious as a Media Lord.

The Marshal of Animations

Festival Organizer · Victim

Responsible for providing live persons for all roles at the Perpetual Animation Festival. When supplies run low ("You had gone through more than a hundred of them already on the morning of this bloody day"), he uses an artificial body and is then forced to sacrifice his own daughter. Both are dismembered, and his severed head delivers a prophetic riddle before the elites dispose of him.

The Marshal's Daughter

Victim · Prophetess

Unnamed young woman forced to play Jezebel when no other "live person" is left. She is dismembered in earnest, and her severed hand delivers an unscripted riddle: "Who thus forgets, in hell or hot: / No drop of blood will be forgot?" The riddle warns that the blood shed for this world's pleasures will not be forgotten.

Oraioi Polloi

Albrecht Fairbrow

Elite · Encourager

Associate of Palgrave Tacoman on Oraioi Polloi. Encourages Palgrave toward the "great creative ocean," the "underlay pit" that is the source of power and influence. Urges: "Dare to create!" His name suggests a "noble brow," a fair-minded appearance that masks demonic counsel.

Aurelion

Devil-Angel · Recording Spirit

The gold-symbol devil-angel, "seventy-ninth recording spirit," who pushes Palgrave's membership application for "this always exciting and ever new cartel that creates." When Palgrave pays the sum, Aurelion accepts him into the "unstable-hundred company of the archetypical devil-angels." His name suggests aureus (gold), and his number, seventy-nine, is the atomic number of gold.

Putty Dwarf

Tempter

A small creature who encourages Palgrave toward Media Lord status alongside Fairbrow. His name suggests malleability and falseness, a creature that takes whatever form the temptation of the moment requires.

Jeanie

Couch Companion

Palgrave Tacoman's couch companion on Oraioi Polloi. Chapter 11 shifts from Janie to Jeanie and places these names in a larger complex of corresponding companions.

The Frame Narrative

Dr. Wilcove Funk / Dr. Vonk

Doctor · Compassionate Observer

Doctor Funk attends Tisman's death; the corresponding Doctor Vonk attends Polder's. Both have a huge head, heavy orbital ridges, a protruding muzzle, and a large back-brain. Funk admits to the compassionate sickness and regards Tisman with sympathy and kindred feeling. Their correspondence is part of the novel's pattern of recurring persons.

Dr. Jude Ravel / Dr. Raphaelson

Doctor · Analyst

Another of the three attending doctors. He and Funk complement each other: "We two would never understand the same half of anything." In the final chapter, as Dr. Raphaelson, he helps analyze the protagonist's composite nature.

Dr. Austin / Dr. August

Doctor

The third attending doctor in both frame narratives. His name shifts slightly between chapters (Austin/August), one instance of the slight displacements between parallel worlds that run through the novel.

The Brigadier of Police

Law Enforcement · Antagonist

Present at both executions. Demands Tisman "expire evenly, quickly, and forever" with no "echo, or any afterglow or after-sound." When Tisman's tone sounds mockingly after death, he shouts "Heads will roll!" He is "firmly under the finger" of Tisman's "one powerful enemy." In the Polder frame, Hector Bogus acts as brigadier.

The Coroner

Death Certifier · Observer

Attends both frame executions. Detects the delta pattern impulses (about three per second) that indicate Tisman is "getting ready for a leap." Suggests alternative death categories: "Possibly, 'Dead, subject to continuance,' or, 'Not so dead as all that.' Alive and dead surely aren't the only two alternatives."

Longram

Good Man · Proxy Victim

A good man whose influence causes barren land to flourish, "one use to which the influence of good men may be put." At Polder's execution, he is the "light companion in death," butchered by mobs to provide spectacle because Polder is "too empty a person to fulfill" the dramatic requirements. He is "disarmed" (his arms torn out), given torture gas, and mutilated, "dying in the brightness of his own disposition."

Commerce & Industry

The Knacker

Fortune Processor · Corpse Handler

A specialist who deals not in dead animal bodies but in "the fortunes and commerces and affairs that were left derelict by the deaths of those bodies." Pilgrim engages him to process the nine fortunes of Evenhand and his henchmen, extracting their wealth for the Holy Knacker statue. He operates in the All-Effects Hall, converting accumulated wealth into gold ingots. A "fine question whether a knacker can be counted as a Lord Spiritual, though often in his business he runs athwart spirits departing."

Melchisedech Duffy

Art Dealer · Collector

Owner of the "Walk-In Bijou in New Orleans," source of excellent artworks loaned to the Daylight Museum. The curator notes: "Melchisedech puts out trash and keeps the good stuff stored away in a lumber room behind." His name recalls the biblical Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem, traditionally read as a type of Christ.

Eidolon & Media Lords

The Eidolon-Masters

Creators · Manipulators

Unnamed beings who constructed the protagonist as "an experimental model." They added "eidolon fiber" to his composition after determining he was "an incurable rogue" and could be used for their purposes. They are the "scrivener devils" or "eidetic devils," about one hundred of them, catalogued "like elements," whose "testaments" form the underlying Group Unconscious or "Folk Ocean" connecting all minds.

Epigraph Sources

Lafferty attributes his chapter epigraphs to invented authors and works as well as to real ones:

Hilaire Belloc (real)
"They order things so damnably in hell." Opens Chapter 10 and links the apparent paradise of the Legacy Worlds to hell.
F. Scott Fitzgerald (real)
"The rich are different from us." Chapter 10 epigraph on the privilege of wealth. The Nine Lives to La Spezia carry this difference into the afterlife.
Clement Goldbeater (fictional)
Author of The Enniscorthy Chronicle. Provides the Chapter 10 epigraph on the Nine Lives to La Spezia, the Legacy Worlds where the rich "are permitted to live nine more lives of pleasure almost hysterical in its immediacy and extent before they go to hell."
Arpad Arutinov (fictional)
Author of The Backdoor of History. Provides Chapter 10 transition: "It is difficult to maintain historical calm in recounting them."
Hound Dog Huckster (fictional)
Provides the second half of the Chapter 7 epigraph: "And when the ritual hounds are done / The dead are you and I."
Endymeon Ellenbogen (fictional)
Author of Arena del Mar. Provides epigraphs on the nature of spectacle and entertainment.
Tractatus (fictional)
Lament of the Times. Provides the epigraph on the making of artificial men, a concern that returns in the doctors' analysis of Polder's body in Chapter 15.

Glossary

Terms, concepts, and Lafferty's invented vocabulary

Characters (65 entries)

del Mar, Maria
A young, taut-faced follower who mourns Pilger Tisman at his burial; her brother Jacob also mourns from a distance. They anticipate Mary and James Morey in the later narrative (12).
Ariel
The post-death manifestation or companion role of Mary Morey, later Moira Mara, paired with her brother James (the hound), as servitors to their cult figure (122, 149, 159, 213). She appears initially as a freckled, brilliant girl in sunlight (150), having lost her wings at the Narrow Corner (129, 160). In the Narrow Corner, she battles the child fire-drake (126) before being destroyed and falling into a pit (129). Also appears with the hound to Palgrave Tacoman (149, 157).
Aurelion
A "gold-symbol demon," the seventy-ninth recording spirit, who pushes applications for membership in the "underlay" cartel controlling power and influence beneath the worlds (148). Membership requires a huge payment, insisted upon by Aurelion (149). Palgrave Tacoman orders the sum paid (149).
Austin, Jon (Doctor)
One of the three "outstanding doctors" attending Pilger Tisman's death-weighing (1). He expresses dislike for Tisman as a "hulk" (4) and questions how Tisman could be loved (4). He notes Tisman leaves behind only one powerful friend and enemy, and wonders about the cult members left behind (6). He is fascinated by the unique colors and light of Tisman's aura, calling the man "a dazzle!" (7). He asks Doctor Funk what Tisman was an adept at (11). He is later listed as one of the cult members present during the final events, referred to as "John Augustine" (103). As Dr. John Augustine, he discusses the nature of Pilgrim's death with Dr. Judas Raffels (117), collaborates in declaring Dusmano dead to collect stipends (118), and makes his way out of life by private conveyance after the others are killed (120). Also appears as "Doctor August" attending Polder Dossman's death (210, 215) and as "Doctor Hans August" analyzing Polder's body (212).
Bed (of Og Scath)
An unusually large iron bed, sofa, or divan, fifteen feet long and six feet wide, located in Og Scath's spacious dwelling; it appears ancient and valuable (176).
Bogus Lords
The meaning ascribed by Hector Bogus to his family name, implying a playful, non-serious participation in the power structures ("Lord play, the big-man play") that only becomes evil when taken seriously (188).
Bogus, Hector
An Eidolon or Media Lord described as technically proficient (180). He engages Polder Dossman in philosophical debate, reveals his power to animate and torture small effigies (181–183), asserts Polder's artificiality (183, 189), modifies the Hand from Heaven (184), and later uses it to kill Polder by dipping him in corrosive sublimate (190). He oversees Polder's final moments, fills the office of brigadier of police (211), and witnesses the analysis of Polder's body (212–214), engaging in a final, contemptuous dialogue with the dying Polder-sliver (214).
Coat of Arms (of Og Scath)
A giant-sized coat of arms hanging in Og Scath's dwelling (176). It bears the name O'Basham (177) and its central image is the Ark with Og riding the roof ridge, holding an umbrella over the main hatch (177).
Consul
A high, anonymous, masked office held sequentially by absolutely good men who head governments and make decisions from behind a veil (69). They must use a "glottle" to disguise their speech (69). If a Consul's face or Consul-name is revealed, he is marked for destruction by devils (70) and public "ritual hounds" (67). The destruction is a national "devil-revel," a pleasure hardly occurring twice a generation (66–67). Cyrus Evenhand is revealed to be the Consul (58, 66), with the code name Rut (49, 76, 89, 94). Pilgrim Dusmano claims being unmasked is an evil omen for a Consul (80) and actively works to bring about Cyrus Evenhand's destruction (50, 66). Pilgrim was once considered for the office but rejected (49). The "masked-Consul system" had previously stabilized rule after a period of assassinations (69).
Consul-Name
The secret name associated with the office of Consul; its revelation leads to the Consul's destruction (70).
Cordcutter
A young Lord Spiritual communicator at the Media Club who informs Pilgrim about the pursuit of Blut, Gut, and Flut, presents a piece of Blut, and seeks more "activating information" from Pilgrim (73–74). He is present at the final cult gathering (103).
Death (of Pilger Tisman)
An execution for "shockingly murderous and irresponsible deeds and behaviors" (1–2). Tisman is sentenced "to die with discomfort" via Yperite or Mustard gas (2). His death is attended by doctors, aides, a coroner, and police, not to save him, but to "weigh his death" using sophisticated and ingenious equipment (1). Tisman is expected to provide a "showy death" as a cult figure but fails, instead experiencing a "death delirium" (2). He successfully "world-jumps," taking his memory, identity, and consciousness-container with him (9–10), leaving behind a mocking, resurrected person-tone (9).
Death (of Polder Dossman)
Attended by Doctor Vonk, Hans August, and Judah Raphaelson, Og Scath (acting coroner), and Hector Bogus (acting brigadier of police) (210). Polder has a "light companion" in death, the proxy Longram (210–211). He is subjected vicariously to Longram's torments (211). His body is analyzed, revealing eidolon fiber, human flesh, and regressed or camel flesh (212). His final moment is the cessation of a "fluttering sliver" of his heart kept active by Bogus (214–215). He is heard screaming eternally from a deep distance, presumed to be in Hell (215).
Dossman, Polder
The final name/identity assumed by the central character after his jump from the Nine Worlds (159). He arrives thirsty and disoriented on a stark, sharp-lined world (159, 161), accompanied by Moira Mara (ariel) and Jake Mara (dog) (159). He establishes commercial success rapidly but struggles with his cult (172–173). He claims high status (Archetype, Zodiac Lord, High Dicer) (201, 203) and performs miracles and wonders (200), including moving a mountain (205), but his power then wanes (206). He is revealed/suspected to be an artificial eidolon-construct (175, 178, 183). He confronts Hector Bogus (180–189) and is subsequently killed via the Hand from Heaven and corrosive sublimate (190), reanimated by galvanic shock (191), and finally dies after a confrontation with hecklers (201–215).
Dusmano, Pilgrim
The central character for much of the narrative. An enigmatic figure who lectures on alternate worlds and controllable world-jumping (15–18), advocating amorality and selective suicide (16–17). He forms a cult, attracting students like the Moreys, Rhinestone Suderman, and Howard Praise (19). He is associated with Noah Zontik (his "powerful friend") (20, 32) and opposed by Cyrus Evenhand (his "powerful enemy") (25). He possesses unusual abilities like flight (24) and passing through walls (24, 25), performs "small miracles" with a scarf (21, 23), and engages in vast, anomalous commerce (33, 41). He manipulates minds (31) and politics (32). He is described as potentially a derivative projection (23, 103), possibly shallow (23), but also an "authentic original" (23). His earlier counterpart Tisman has a distinctive call-tone and aura (6–7); Pilgrim has the familiar dripping hands (115). He kills Hut (38), ritually dispatches the Pym family as messengers (53–55), confronts the spy Trenchant (79–83), and is later revealed as the target for destruction by the Media Lords (108) before being pursued and killed by militia and horses (114–118). (See also Dossman, Polder for his later identity).
Evenhand, Cyrus
Pilgrim Dusmano's primary antagonist, designated his "one powerful enemy" (6, 25, 86). He is the leader of a powerful and secret organization (27) employing eight henchmen with code names (25, 48–49). Operating behind a mask (26), he holds the anonymous office of the Consul (58, 66), with the code name Rut (49). Accounted a good, spotless, and saintly man (25, 49, 66, 71), he conducts his off-world commerce via "blissful permit" (90). Pilgrim targets him for destruction despite his goodness (50), leaks his identity (58), inciting national hysteria (66–68). Cyrus Evenhand listens in on Pilgrim's conversations (76) and is later killed and dismembered by the Media Lords or the populace (108), his vast fortunes becoming derelict (89, 94).
Fairfronter, Lord
An older, elegant Lord Spiritual and member of Pilgrim Dusmano's inner cult, recognizable by the rare "Golden Shovel Pip" and "Pilgrim Staff" he wears (75). He expresses anxiety about Dusmano leaving the world, praises his advancement of posthuman personality, questions the timing, and asks about a replacement leader (75). He pledges to incorporate Dusmano's sayings into the cult (78) and inquires about arrangements for Dusmano's desired death (78). He later cautions Dusmano to be careful, calling him their only cult figure (78). Present at the final cult gathering (103), he questions whether Dusmano is a Christus sending a Paraclete (104), disputes Judas Raffels' claim about green-thorn time being out of season (112), and cautions Judas Raffels about the subjectivity of his visions (106).
Fairbrow, Albrecht
An elite companion of Palgrave Tacoman and Jeanie on Oraioi Polloi (147). Though described by the narrator as one of the "deeply evil men" (148), he compliments Lorica on killing the first boar (153). He is assigned by Palgrave to hunt the second, dangerous "scurrying boar" (154), but his horse's legs are broken, and he is killed by the boar while fighting on foot (155). His death scene matches an image previously displayed on the post boy's horn, and his dead face resembles Palgrave's (155).
False Lord Spiritual
The designation applied to the spy Trenchant, implying he held credentials but lacked the true essence or status of a Lord Spiritual (79, 184). Identified as such by Pilgrim (83), he is seized by genuine Media Lords and killed by Pilgrim (83). His leftover pieces are later collected (84).
Fineface, Albert
Spokesman and captain of the elites on Cannes World. He investigates the Jezebel performance, wounds the Marshal's tongue, and acts as broker for Pelion Tuscamondo's publication in the Group Unconscious (137–144). Albrecht Fairbrow and later Leslie Whitebread occupy related roles on Oraioi Polloi.
Funk, Wilcove (Doctor)
One of the three physicians overseeing Pilger Tisman's death-weighing (1). He provides commentary on Tisman's state ("frustrated-in-death," "betrayed-in-death cult figure") (2), death-weighing procedures (3), Tisman's aura and call-tone (4), and his own large head and back-brain (4–5). He monitors Tisman's cerebral juglans (5), discusses afterlife topology (9), and potentially conceals the "compensating thing" Tisman leaves (10). Later appears as Doctor Vonk attending Polder Dossman's death (210), offering analysis (211–212) and confirming Og Scath's death (214).
Holy Knacker
The name bestowed by Mary Morey upon the golden statue formed from the eviscerated and gold-filled body of the knacker (101). The statue captures the knacker’s final, paradoxical expression of "strangest compassion" (99). The term also refers to a hulking, apelike entity encountered in the Narrow Corner after death (122, 123). This being, identified as the flesh-smith and body-smith (126), smells inexplicably of molten gold treated with lime flux (131) and declares the finality of results in that realm (132) after being thrown into the pit by Polder (131).
Hound
The post-death manifestation or companion role of James Morey, paired with his sister Mary/Moira (the ariel), as servitors to their cult figure (122, 159, 213). He appears as a somber, faithful, human-form dog dwelling in shadow (150). He assembles hound-form dogs for hunting (151). After death, he battles Wut in the Narrow Corner (128) before being destroyed and falling into the abyss, his howls echoing from the depths (129).
JACOB DEL MAR
The brother of Maria del Mar and, like her, a follower of the cult figure Pilger Tisman (12). He mourns Tisman's death at the burial, keeping his distance but exhibiting silent, sobbing motion (12).
JAKE MARA
The name given to James Morey in the later stages of the narrative, after Polder Dossman's arrival in the stark, sharp-lined world (162). He is described as a "wan-wit young man" whose brains were scrambled during his time as a dog (162). He retains his loyalty to Polder, offering practical assistance like locating an "umbrella merchant" (Lorica) (167) and gathering intelligence on the hecklers (202). He expresses concern for Polder's well-being, protesting when doctors plan to disassemble him (195) and when the knacker proposes documenting his potential prophetic appearance (93).
JANIE
Pelion Tuscamondo's frequent companion on Cannes World (139). Possessing jeweled eyes and a jeweled mind (140), she is depicted with the "stereotyped perfection" of bright women within the Legacy (139). She precipitates a scandal at the Cannes Perpetual Animation Festival by exposing the use of an automaton instead of a live actress in the Jezebel drama (134, 137). She also acts as an intermediary, informing Pelion of a waiting visitor (145). See also JEANIE, JANIE-JEANIE.
JEANIE
Palgrave Tacoman's companion in a loge on Oraioi Polloi (147). She alerts Palgrave to the arrival of the ariel and the dog (Moira and Jake) (149). Seems to be the same character as JANIE.
JANIE-JEANIE
The paired form Janie-Jeanie marks the shift between the couch companions of Pelion and Palgrave at the opening of Chapter 11 (145).
Knacker
A specialist initially defined as dealing with animal carcasses (88), but the specific, talented individual engaged by Pilgrim Dusmano primarily processes the derelict fortunes, commerces, and affairs of the dead or soon-to-be-dead, such as Consul Cyrus Evenhand and his eight associates (88–89). This knacker, potentially a Lord Spiritual (89), uses advanced, possibly supernatural documentation techniques involving numinosity (93) and "intuitive illogic" (95) to consolidate these vast, multi-world assets (90, 94). He operates out of the All-Effects Hall (90) and claims descent from a lineage possessing secret knowledge (93). Asserting his claim ("It's all mine") to the Mut Cult's gold (96), he is betrayed by Pilgrim and killed by Mary Morey and James Morey, who eviscerate him and fill his body with molten gold; the gilded corpse becomes the HOLY KNACKER statue (97–101). He reappears post-death as an entity in the Narrow Corner (122).
Longram
A good man to whom utterly barren land (Longram's Acres) had been ceded, which then flourished under his influence before being taken away again (206). He serves as Polder Dossman's "light companion" or proxy in death, having been "butchered by the mobs" and subjected to mutilation and torture gas, fulfilling the dramatic requirements Polder is too empty to meet (211). He is certainly dead before Polder's final end (213).
Lord of the Worlds
A divine or supreme entity. Apparently does not always know the best course regarding its own devices (20). Put tongues, fingers, styli, ethereal tinsel, ears, eyes, and the "perverse lobe" in humans for communication and subversion (107). Polder and Moira Mara seek means to convince the Lord of the Worlds of Polder's goodness (176).
Lorica
An adept and powerful man who sells worlds, systems, and galaxies, but is dismissed as an umbrella peddler (147–149). He warns Palgrave against buying archetypal membership in the infernal cartel and offers free participation in transcendence instead. Fairbrow and the Putty Dwarf undermine him. During the boar hunt he kills the first boar after his horse is impaled (152–153).
Mara, Jake
The name used for James Morey after Polder Dossman arrives in the stark, sharp-lined world (162). He is described as "wanwit," his brains having been scrambled (162). He accompanies Polder and Moira (162), locates the "umbrella merchant" Lorica (167), provides intelligence about the hecklers (202), and protests the planned "disassembly" of Polder (195).
Mara, Moira
The name used for Mary Morey after Polder Dossman arrives in the stark, sharp-lined world (162). She accompanies Polder and Jake (162), takes Polder's orders for investments and renting a grotto (164, 165, 166), attempts to manage Polder's cult affairs (172), asserts the necessity of belief in Polder's exaggerated status (198), gives Hector Bogus orders for Polder's glorification (192), critiques Polder's fear (208), and critiques the coin flip prank (209).
Marshal of Animations
The official responsible for ensuring live actors are used in the Cannes Perpetual Animation Festival (134). He is dragged before the elites after an automaton is used for Jezebel (137), confesses under duress that he substituted his own daughter due to a lack of other available actresses (138), and is subsequently beheaded and disarmed (139). A new Marshal is appointed (139).
Masked-Consul System
The governmental structure preceding the narrative's main timeline, established after a period of assassinations, which relied on anonymous, masked Consuls making decisions from behind a veil (69).
Morey, James
The brother of Mary Morey (60). Often observed lingering in the shadows while Mary occupies the sunlight, leading to speculation that he is her shadow (60). Despite recognizing Pilgrim Dusmano's artificiality, he stays a leading member of the Dusmano cult (71). He acts as an assistant to Pilgrim, filling a crock with water to drown the statuette with Pilgrim's former eyes (63) and later operating the hoist and furnace during the ritual creation of the Holy Knacker statue (97, 99, 100). He is awed and frightened by the statue's unnatural glow (101). Afterward, James finds the "gold lust and the blood lust" drain out of him, leaving him sobbing silently in the shadows (101). He sometimes speaks "out of the shadows," offering observations on Dusmano's nature (62) or the state of the drowning statuette (67). He attends the final cult gathering (103) and affirms the belief in Pilgrim's eventual return in a parallel form (104). After his death alongside Mary, he manifests as the HOUND servitor in the afterlife (122). See also Mara, Jake.
Morey, Mary
A student and leading follower of Pilgrim Dusmano, sister of James Morey. She helps create the Holy Knacker, follows Pilgrim into death, and appears as the ariel in the Narrow Corner. In the later sharp-lined world she is Moira Mara. Her devotion includes clear recognition of Pilgrim's cruelty and artificiality (18–19, 60–71, 92–101, 112–129, 162–209).
Muckman, Randal
A multimedia reporter contacted by Pilgrim Dusmano via voxo (57). Pilgrim gives him the information "Cyrus Evenhand is Consul" (58). Muckman attributes the information to a "high, wide. . . and handsome source" (knowing it to be the devious Pilgrim) and broadcasts it, triggering the main crisis (58). He is later present at the final cult gathering in the windowless room (103).
Music, Clarence
The curator of the Daylight Museum (61, 103). He engages with Pilgrim Dusmano and the Moreys about art, shadows, sanity, and the nature of the Consul (61–63, 66–67, 69–71). He is present during the final cult gathering (103) and asks why the two Doctors Medical are drawn to Pilgrim (106).
Pilgrim Staff
A rare insignia, "smaller than a mote in the eye," worn by Lord Fairfronter (along with the Golden Shovel Pip), signifying his connection to the Dusmano cult and his dedication to establishing the Pilgrim image (75, 84).
Pilgrim, Peter (of Myth)
A legendary figure whom the spy Trenchant accuses Pilgrim Dusmano of not being, calling Dusmano a "falser Pilgrim" (82). This accusation strikes Dusmano, forcing him to confront his own authenticity in the "postreason era" (82). Hector Bogus also refers to this figure when challenging Polder's identity (185).
Polder-Sliver
The last remnant of Polder Dossman, a fluttering piece of his heart, kept animate and tortured by Hector Bogus in a cabinet before finally ceasing (214–215).
Praise, Howard
Initially a student hesitant about Pilgrim Dusmano's chaotic nature (16, 19), he is nonetheless compelled into the cult (19). He is still a member at the final events (103), stoutly defying the militia before Judas Raffels betrays Pilgrim's location (114), and mutters about "Heavy footsteps" approaching (113).
Putty Dwarf
An entity present with Lorica and Albrecht Fairbrow on Oraioi Polloi (148). He argues that all things become "putty" in the hands of those who join the "great creative ocean" (148), dismisses Lorica as common (148), and promotes the value of "antilife" (149).
Pym Family (Wife, Elder Child, Younger Child)
Aubrey Pym's wife is initially enthusiastic about transferring (39), the elder child is compliant (53), but the younger child is defiant and preternaturally hostile (40, 53–55). All three are ritually killed by Pilgrim with the stone knife after Aubrey's death, to accompany him as "strings" on his mission to Supply (54–55). Their bodies are disposed of in the grindershredder (56). The younger child reappears as a malevolent entity in the Narrow Corner afterlife (122, 124, 126, 128, 129).
Pym, Aubrey
An employee in Pilgrim Dusmano's commerce division (33). Approaching Pilgrim nervously, he asks for a raise (33–34). Pilgrim designates him as a messenger to Supply, using Pym's wife and two children as "hostages" (34). He is dispatched with his family to Dongola via a ritual involving apprehension, an invisible bridge, and throat-cutting with a stone knife (38–39, 53).
Raffels, Judas (Doctor Medical)
One of the eleven cult members present during the final gathering (103). He challenges Lord Fairfronter's interpretation of Pilgrim (106), expresses disbelief in spirits but interest in Pilgrim's mutable medical body and detached shadow (106). He develops a new talent for remote viewing (108, 111), reports on Cyrus Evenhand's death and the shift of the Lords' attention to Pilgrim (108–109). He betrays Pilgrim's hiding place to the militia (114) and whistles "Heads Will Roll" as he leaves with them (114). Along with John Augustine (Doctor), he declares Dusmano dead and receives chits for stipends (118), and later pronounces Mary Morey dead for the same purpose (119). He is then killed by the militia with horses after Noah Zontik (120).
Raphaelson, Judah (Doctor)
One of the three outstanding doctors attending the death-weighing of Polder Dossman (210). He questions the nature of Polder's physical composition (212) and notes the finality of Polder's "last jump" (215).
Ravel, Jude (Doctor)
One of the three "outstanding doctors" attending Pilger Tisman's death-weighing (1). He comments on Tisman enduring pain well, discusses animal death rituals (2); Doctor Funk comments on the failure to deliver a showy death. He admires Tisman's complex and powerful call-tone (6) and explains how the tone might signal Tisman's successful escape after death (7). He whistles the tune "Heads Will Roll" after Tisman's successful jump and the brigadier's threats (10). He muses on the erasure of Tisman's brain data after the jump (10–11).
Scath, Oak
The name used by the young lad Polder Dossman encounters in Camel Town (168). He claims to be ancient Og, who rode the Ark (172, 177), is primordial (176), and was tasked before Polder's arrival with watching over and protecting him, holding the metaphorical umbrella (168, 172). He possesses unusual knowledge (e.g., seeing the writing on brick fragments in Polder's mind) (172), facilitates Polder's business (178), but stubbornly resists promoting Polder's cult, finding it not "serious" or "funny enough" (173, 174). He confirms Polder has achieved archetype status (197), warns him against the mountain-moving challenge (204), but still asserts his role as protector (203). He later attends Polder's death as acting coroner (210), questions the doctors about Polder's composite nature (212), feels Polder's thought about Prime World (213), witnesses the final flutter (214), and dies suddenly as well, possibly accompanying Polder "an instant early" (214). See also Scath, Og.
Scath, Og
The primordial identity claimed by Oak Scath (172, 176, 177). He is Polder Dossman's designated protector (168, 172), acting as his "shield" (203). Possesses "type-memory" regarding Merope's forms (197). Fulfills the role of coroner at Polder's death (210). See also Scath, Oak.
SCATH, OG/OAK
See Scath, Oak and Scath, Og.
SCENT (OF PILGRIM)
Used metaphorically by Randal Muckman to identify Pilgrim Dusmano as the probable source of information ("From a knowledgeable man whose dishonesty few doubt" would have the scent of Pilgrim all over it) (58).
SPURGEON
An associate and employee heading Pilgrim Dusmano's Commerce division (35). He nervously brings up the recurring, forgotten issue of needing adjustments from Supply (35). He reveals he arrived at his position less than a year prior as an "outre messenger" from Supply, though he forgot the details (36). He oversees the drawing up of the "bill of particulars" for the messenger (37, 51). Later present at the final cult gathering (103) and asks why Pilgrim should hide (111). He follows the militia out with Raffels, Zontik, and the Moreys (116).
Suderman, Rhinestone
A large, fair-haired female student of Pilgrim Dusmano (18). Although claiming not to understand or be attracted to him, she acknowledges his correctness (18) and initiates the formation of the Pilgrim Dusmano cult, suggesting "chaos" as its organizing principle (19). She is present at the final cult gathering (103), mourns Pilgrim's departure (104), and questions Judas Raffels (Doctor) about his new psychic abilities (108).
Tacoman, Palgrave
An identity of the main character, seemingly during his time on the Nine World of Oraioi Polloi (146). He is attended by Jeanie and Albrecht Fairbrow (147), interacts with Lorica (147–149) and the Putty Dwarf (148–149), orders the summoning of mountains for a backdrop (141), and becomes recognized as an archetype associated with a new unstable element and the camel totem (154). He participates in a ritual boar hunt (152), witnesses Albrecht Fairbrow's death (155), confronts the King Boar (156), and experiences a ritual death mirroring the scene on the post boy's horn, becoming a "very good Adonis" (157). His associate aspects continue pleasuring themselves across the Nine Worlds after this death (157).
Tisman, Pilger
The cult figure executed with Yperite at the opening of the novel. Doctors Funk, Austin, and Ravel monitor his death, but he carries away memory and identity. His person-tone sounds triumphantly after bodily death, and Funk conceals something left behind by the departure (1–12).
Trenchant
A young Lord Spiritual from the Provinces with a "furtive look" and the "heart of a squeamish spy" (79). He challenges Pilgrim Dusmano at the Media Club, questioning his authenticity and the validity of his cult (79, 82). He is called the "Rubber Knife" (79); in the later world, Polder identifies Hector Bogus as his counterpart (184). Trenchant is seized by other Media Lords and killed by Pilgrim (83).
Tuscamondo, Pelion
An identity of the main character, apparently during his time on the Nine World of Cannes (139, 146). He is depicted as handsome, with a powerful yet intricate voice, possessing a shimmer or dazzle, and known as the hypnotic, electric, magnetic, or transcendent man with dripping hands (139). He is accompanied by Janie (139), watches multiple dramas (140), orders mountains for a backdrop (141), and makes a deal with Albert Fineface to publish his "personal flame and image" into the collective unconscious (141–144).
Vonk, Doctor
One of the three outstanding doctors attending the death-weighing of Polder Dossman (210). He possesses a huge head, heavy orbital ridges, a protruding muzzle making a chin impossible, a large back-brain, and great good humor; described as a tremendous man with animal vitality and an expert analyst (211). He comments on Polder's composite nature (human, regressed flesh, eidolon fiber) (212), confirms Og Scath's death (214), and notes the failure of Polder's final "flutter" (215). (Seems identical to Wilcove Funk (Doctor) from Pilger Tisman's death.)
Whitebread, Leslie
An elite figure on Oraioi Polloi who becomes the designated spokesman after Albrecht Fairbrow's death (155). He orders the ariel and dog attendees whipped away from the deceased Palgrave Tacoman (157).
Wiggly-Word Lord
Polder Dossman's angry, dismissive epithet for Hector Bogus, grouping him with Eidetic, Media, and Advocate Lords (185).
Zodiac Lord
A high status attainable within the esoteric structures of Polder Dossman's world (197). Polder considers becoming a "double Lord of the Zodiac" representing the reconstituted signs of the camel and the boar (174). Og Scath asserts Polder has become one (197), a status Polder later claims (201, 203). Membership signifies integration into the archetypal patterns underlying reality (197). Hector Bogus questions the validity of Polder's claim (197).
Zontik, Noah
The figure described as Pilgrim Dusmano's "one powerful friend" (20, 27, 86) and associate (20). He holds the titles of both Lord Temporal and Lord Spiritual (84), wears the insignia of the Golden Shovel and the Pilgrim Staff (84), and is known professionally as "the Umbrella" for his services in shielding and protection (28, 103). He is tasked by God with protecting Pilgrim, even into Hell (27), a commission he feels compelled to honor despite his disbelief (84, 104). He frequently challenges Pilgrim's actions and philosophy, accusing him of being a derivative projection (23) and warning him of danger (85, 110). He is also assigned to protect Cyrus Evenhand (86). He belongs to the Dusmano cult (84, 103) but struggles with its implications (84, 103–105). He witnesses Pilgrim's final decline (110) and follows him into death, stating Pilgrim will need his "umbrella" protection wherever he goes (119); he is subsequently killed by the militia with horses (120).

Locations (49 entries)

All-Effects Hall
An armored and secluded facility behind the Golden Grotto of the Pilgrim Cult, used for the "knacker business of harvesting fortunes" (90). Mary Morey and James Morey work there, overseeing furnaces for golden images and machinery (90). It has a bright light (100), ponderous doorways connecting to the Grotto (100), and a skylike height where the gilded knacker statue is hung (100). The knacker demands the Mut Cult gold be brought there (92), and the Moreys use a dray to transport it (94, 95). The final transformation and display of the knacker statue occur within or just outside it (99–101).
Arena
The setting for the three-tiered conflict in the Narrow Corner after death (125). Also mentioned regarding Roman games (70). The arena, village, and world are identical in Adobe Pueblos (147).
Aspect World
A type of alternate reality, distinct from outer worlds, suggested by Mut as the origin of Pilgrim Dusmano (50). Messages are sent to other aspects via messenger families (55). Pilgrim Dusmano speaks of parallel Dusmanos on alternate worlds or aspects (89).
Atrium Theater
Location in Oraioi Polloi where the "living theaters" of the Nine Worlds to La Spezia are presented (147). The "Adoration of the Boar" is performed there (157).
Ballad, World-Jumper's
A short verse serving as an epigraph, contemplating mortality and the precarious nature of existence on a world from which one might abruptly depart (1). Also quoted by Polder Dossman near his end (210).
Boondocks World
Hector Bogus's dismissive term for Prime World (213) and the world where Polder's final death occurs (214).
Camel Town
A location described by a local lad as the "second-best town in the world in every way," best in nothing but second-best in everything, like the camel (163–164). Polder visits it upon arrival in a sharp-lined, simple world (163).
Cannes
One of the nine locations constituting the Nine Worlds to La Spezia, part of the Legacy of the rich (134, 146).
Cannes Perpetual Animation Festival
An ongoing event on Cannes World requiring the constant use of live actors for its ten thousand daily dramas (135). Elite lifetimes are measured by the cycle of these dramas (135). Features dramas based on Doré illustrations, including Jehu's Companions Finding the Remains of Jezebel (135).
Corner, Narrow
See Narrow Corner.
Curator (Daylight Museum)
Clarence Music (103). He interacts with Pilgrim Dusmano and the Moreys, discussing Pilgrim's shadows and sanity (61), explaining the museum's rules (59), revealing items from the Duffy Walk-In Bijou (63), handling the Jezebel note (66), expressing bewilderment at the persecution of the Consul (66–67), and referring to the Consul's eyepiece (69). He is initially described as fearful but drawn to the "blood-magnet" (70) and later as "straight corned mutton" for his naive view of the populace (68).
Daylight Museum
A museum favoring art that is "uncompromised and untrammeled," featuring "plain abundance" and no "dark corners" or "dark concepts" (59). It emphasizes clear representation and chaste colors, with rules against art inducing fever or excessive unease (59). Pilgrim Dusmano frequents it, partly to create his own "special image" (59). It houses works by Groben (63), van Gregory Ghi (66), Alessandro (66), Scanlon, Adam (65), Finnegan (65), and a triptych by "Joe Smith" (65). The curator is Clarence Music (61). Pilgrim has a report about Cyrus Evenhand delivered outside it (58) and later discusses art and the Consul with the curator and the Moreys inside (60–71).
Delectable
One of the nine locations making up the Nine Worlds to La Spezia (134, 146).
Drag-World Gravity
One of the forces seemingly, but not actually, present at the commodity arrival floor (42).
Dummies (on a World)
From the "World-Jumper's Ballad," one of the stances humans take: "We stand like dummies on a world / Or be like sharpies jumping off it" (1).
Fetish World
Pilgrim Dusmano's term for Prime World, emphasizing its oppressive materiality where metaphors are concrete, reality is rigidly literal, and "compensation is calculated and extracted" (21).
First World
The originating or primary reality in a series of worlds. Pilgrim Dusmano speaks of counterworlds having "no first world" (117).
Fortean World
Named by Noah Zontik as one aspect of the Prime World of prime people, alongside the uninfused, grubby, spiritualist, and quack aspects (23).
Furnaces (in All-Effects Hall)
Equipment used for casting golden images, managed by the Moreys (90). James uses one, already fired by Pilgrim, to melt down the Mut Cult gold (97). A separate "flashfurnace" contains molten gold for plating the knacker's corpse (98, 100).
Golden Grotto
The ornate front section or public face of the Pilgrim Cult headquarters, located before the armored All-Effects Hall (90, 94). The gilded knacker statue is rolled out into the Grotto for display (100), and James Morey frequently stands in its shadows (101).
Grotto, Golden
See Golden Grotto.
Grubby World
One of the aspects of the Prime World of prime people, according to Noah Zontik (23).
Hy-Brasail
One of the nine locations comprising the Nine Worlds to La Spezia, part of the exclusive Legacy of the rich (134, 146).
La Spezia
The ninth named world of the Legacy, alongside Cannes, Oraioi Polloi, Hy-Brasail, Smart Set, Savona, Delectable, Theleme, and Luogo Perfetto. It is not a last chronological stage: the Nine Lives exist outside time and are never exhausted (133–146, 157).
Lad (in Camel Town)
A bright, young, local resident of Camel Town who engages Polder Dossman in a detailed conversation about the unique "second-best" status of camels and of Camel Town (163–167). He appears skeptical but impressed by Polder's Hand from Heaven display (163). He sells Polder his last camel (167) and reveals he has been "renovated," was likely an older man previously, and has been waiting for Polder (167). He identifies himself as Oak Scath (168).
Legacy
Specifically refers to the Nine Lives to La Spezia, a special compensation granted to the rich, permitting them nine additional lives of "almost hysterical" pleasure after death before potentially going to hell (133). This Legacy consists of Nine Moments (or momentums/powers), not segments of time (140), existing outside of time (160). The nine associated worlds (Cannes, Oraioi Polloi, HyBrasail, Smart Set, Savona, Delectable, Theleme, Luogo Perfetto, La Spezia) form a rivière or promontory shape (134). The "restrictive covenants" of the Legacy involve nine rich lives and worlds described as "pleasant little pieces of eternity" (132). Also mentioned is an "unusual Legacy" through which the pan-morph possesses nine special changes (127). Polder Dossman inherits a legacy via the Hand from Heaven gesture (168). Janie is described as one of the bright women who share in the Legacy (139).
Lives (Nine Lives to La Spezia)
The rich's Legacy of nine lives or aspects of intense pleasure. These are nine Moments or powers without contact with time, not sequential lives that are exhausted. They persist even when another aspect of the person is in hell (133–146, 157, 208).
Luogo Perfetto
One of the nine worlds or states constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia (134, 146).
Media Club
An exclusive club where Pilgrim Dusmano holds honored membership (72). He dines there on mock-pizzle pie (75) and later consumes the roasted flesh of the henchman Blut (87). He interacts with various Lords Spiritual (Cordcutter, Fairfronter, Trenchant) within its premises (73–83) before fleeing from it near the narrative's end (110).
Museum
Several are mentioned: the Daylight Museum (59, 60, 61, 63, 65, 66, 106), the Dismal Den (59, 60), the Implosion House (59), Tom Fool's (59), and the Introspection Inn (59). Pilgrim Dusmano frequents museums as part of constructing his public image (59).
Museum-Munchers' Daybook
The source of the epigraph for Chapter 5 ("An idol-thing with jewel eyes. . .") (57).
Narrow Corner
A location in the afterlife province known as the Iron Meadows or the Camel's Eye (121). It is depicted as a treacherous, pulsating, steep pass (124) formed not by hands but by the projected intuitions of countless bruised and dislocated souls (127), influenced by figures like Alighieri, Christ in Matthew, Maugham, Blake, Demetriades/Finnegan, and Ovyde (127). Legends describe it as a knife-edge precipice of glare ice (or molten rock) flanked by bottomless chasms where tooth-clattering spirits wait to devour souls and slake revenges (125). It is the setting for a chaotic battle involving the pan-morphic Pilgrim/Polder, the ariel, the dog, the Holy Knacker (body-smith), Wut (maniac), and the Pym child (fire-drake) (122–131). The body-smith attempts to trap Pilgrim there in a final form (126), and Polder falls into its chasm (132).
Nine Lives to La Spezia
The special Legacy of the rich: nine lives of intense pleasure in worlds outside time. The apparent promise of nine lives before hell is qualified by the insistence that nobody ever uses them up. Nine aspects continue in pleasure even while a tenth suffers elsewhere (133–146, 157, 208).
Nine Worlds to La Spezia
The collection of nine distinct locations or states (Cannes, Oraioi Polloi, Hy-Brasail, Smart Set, Savona, Delectable, Theleme, Luogo Perfetto, La Spezia) that constitute the Nine Lives legacy (134, 146). They exist outside of time and leave no memory (160). Death within them is a "pleasant coma" (157). Polder Dossman seeks confirmation of his presence within them (208). Hector Bogus confirms Polder is present nine times across the Nine Worlds (208). Polder is asked by Bogus if he seeks to return there from what he believes to be Prime World (207).
Oraioi Polloi
One of the nine worlds constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia legacy (134, 146). It features the Atrium Theater where dramas like the Resurrection of Lazarus and the Adoration of the Boar are presented (147, 157). Death there is described as a "pleasant coma" (157). Palgrave Tacoman, Jeanie, Albrecht Fairbrow, and Lorica are present there (147).
Patsy World
Polder Dossman's suspected assessment of the sharp-lined world where Polder arrives, anticipating easy exploitation ("patsy-picking time") (166).
Postanarchic (Age/Era/World)
The time period or state of reality in which much of the narrative occurs (80, 94, 105, 175, 197). Characterized by the rejection of overt rule, the necessity of masked authority (Consul), the power of Media Lords, the rise of cults, and a pervasive "age of unreason" (81, 105). Thieves' honor is considered "patchy" in this era (97). Noah Zontik suggests it is a peculiar state, possibly not entered by most worlds (105). Pilgrim/Polder is considered potentially the "correct godlet" for this age (105).
Present World
The term used to distinguish the current reality from other worlds or aspects, such as Dongola (55).
Prime World
A hypothetical foundational reality (20). Described by Pilgrim Dusmano as the potential "narrow foul chance" or downside to world-jumping (20), the dullest possible world, where mythology is sordid reality, compensation is extracted, facts are hard without buoyancy, metaphors are material, and logic is absolute delirium (21). It is murk, mud, miasmic fever, featuring sinewy gripping hands and a low sky (21). Escape is impossible, with only two ways off: one being Hell (21). It's the anchor of eschatological things (21). Worrying about being on Prime World is a sign of its influence (183). Og Scath believes Polder thought he was on Prime World when he died (213). Polder fears he might fall into Hell from it (206, 208). Moira Morey argues probability proves their current world isn't Prime World (208).
Quack World
One of the enumerated aspects defining the nature of the Prime World of prime people, listed alongside the uninfused, grubby, spiritualist, and Fortean worlds (23).
SAVONA
One of the nine worlds or states constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia legacy (134, 146).
SCENES (OFF-THIS-WORLD / OUT-OF-MIND)
Deep, abiding, reflected images flickering in Noah Zontik's eyes when looking at Pilgrim Dusmano (or in Og Scath's eyes looking at Polder Dossman), depicting events that happened long ago and far away, often to other people (parallel persons) rather than the observers or the observed (32, 175).
SHARPIES (JUMPING OFF A WORLD)
In the opening “World-Jumper's Ballad,” sharpies are the clever ones who jump off a world, contrasted with dummies who stay upon it (1).
SMART SET
One of the nine worlds or states constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia legacy (134, 146).
SPIRITUALIST WORLD
One of the aspects defining the Prime World of prime people, according to Noah Zontik (23).
Theleme
One of the nine worlds or states constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia legacy (134, 146).
Town
Several are mentioned: Camel Town (163); Dongola (39); the small town at the base of the hill in the sharp-lined world (162); the small town near Jerusalem where Lazarus might have been resurrected (141).
World-Jumper / World-Jumping
The act of transitioning between alternate worlds or realities, often at the moment of death (11, 16). Pilger Tisman is a successful world-jumper (11), utilizing a personal "trick" (8) involving the delta brain pattern (8) to evade capture by the death-monitors' "nets" (7, 11) and take "weighable substance" (memory, identity, consciousness) with him (10). The process allows practiced individuals to select destinations or return to specific life stages (17), though a slow or badly handled death can result in a "bad jump" (113, 118). Polder Dossman makes a successful, though rough, jump resulting in "Resurrection Blues" (159). It is distinct from Pilger Tisman's earlier practice as a "body-jumper" (106). The process is sometimes referred to as transmigration or metacosmosis (16).
World-Jumper's Ballad
The source of epigraphs contemplating mortality and transition, containing the lines "We stand like dummies on a world / Or be like sharpies jumping off it" (1) and describing the "end of jumping" (210).

Cosmology (180 entries)

Abridgments
Concentrated essences of memory stored within the cerebral juglans or "remembering acorn" (5). Pilger Tisman's memory center, filled with these, is still intact immediately after death but collapses shortly thereafter as its content is stolen (9).
Absolute Logic
The defining characteristic of Prime World, described by Pilgrim Dusmano as the "absolute logic of total delirium," the most fearful thing to be found anywhere (21).
Accounts, Ultimate
Records kept meticulously on Prime World, associated with logic, compensation, and a narrow, one-dimensional sequence; Pilgrim Dusmano expresses fear of having to "pay" them (20).
Acorn, Remembering
See Juglans, Cerebral (5).
After-Appearances
Ghostly manifestations, often harmless in earlier times, resulting from individuals carrying minimal personal baggage (memory, identity, consciousness) forward from death (3). Contrasted with the more disruptive "horrendous ghost worlds" erected by later, trickier departing cult figures (4).
Afterglow / After-Sound
Lingering traces of a person after death, specifically the person-tone, which the brigadier of police does not want to perceive after Pilger Tisman's execution (6, 7).
Alternate Worlds
Multiple, co-existing realities theorized by various groups. Scientists posited billions scattered through space (13), while "fringies and nonsuches" correctly believed they occupied the same familiar local space as "tree-worlds" or "branch-worlds" (14). Pilgrim Dusmano reconciled these views, claiming billions exist "right here right now," viewable through a "tri-mental view," with distant galaxies being mere marginalia (15). These worlds allow for "world-jumping" or "transmigration" (16), potentially controllable to repeat or select specific life experiences or ages (16–17), including unusual environs (17). Dusmano claims they are only "about as real as the world we're in now" (17). Some are considered parallel (30, 77, 78, 104). They can be broken "like eggs" by passage through them (104).
Alternate Worlds / Multiplicity of Reality
The narrative's basic metaphysical assertion, positing the co-existence of countless realities. Initial theories range from billions of worlds scattered through conventional space (13) to billions occupying the same local space ("tree-worlds," "branch-worlds") (14). Pilgrim Dusmano synthesizes these, claiming billions exist "right here right now," perceivable through a "tri-mental view," rendering distant galaxies mere marginalia (15). This multiplicity enables WorldJumping or "transmigration," potentially allowing selection of desired realities or life stages (16–17), and underpins Dusmano's philosophy where conventional morality, consequence, and even death are rendered illusory (16). These worlds possess varying degrees of reality ("about as real as the world we're in now") (17) and include specialized environs (17) and the distinct afterlife sequence of the Nine Worlds to La Spezia (133–134). Set against this multiplicity is the single, dreaded Prime World, the potential anchor of reality and feared gateway to damnation (20–21). Much of the novel's speculation turns on movement among these realities, whether by jumps or by psychic leakage (32), and on their uncertain status.
Amalgamated Camel Enterprises
The only aspect of Polder Dossman's affairs that Og Scath admits to promoting (174).
Amorality
Stated by Pilgrim Dusmano to be a "total thing" implicit in his claim regarding alternate worlds, rendering recompense, debt, guilt, punishment, and death mere illusions (16).
Anchor (of Final Things)
Prime World is described as the base and anchor of the four final or eschatological things (21).
Antilogy
Loved by Pilgrim Dusmano, in contrast to logy or logic, which he blinds his eyes to (117).
Ape-Man
An aspect or description of the Holy Knacker/fleshsmith/body-smith encountered in the Narrow Corner (126, 127, 131).
Archetype
A fundamental pattern or figure. Palgrave Tacoman becomes one of the "archetypical devil-angels" upon the billionfold multiplication of his testament (154). Polder Dossman claims this status (201, 203), along with being a Zodiac Lord and High Dicer (203). Og Scath affirms Polder has become one, located in the underlying ocean of minds (197), but Hector Bogus dismisses him as merely a "little green eidolon-godling" (197). Palgrave is initially reluctant to become one (147). The term is also linked to the "communicating gods of the atomic numbers" (154).
Artificial
A descriptor applied to various entities and concepts. Pilgrim Dusmano suggests the ancient pleasures are lost and modern organized rituals are artificial (71). He claims his parallel selves ("sticks") are artificial personalities (77). Polder Dossman is suspected of being artificial, potentially a "made-thing" of the Eidetic Lords (175), an "artificial contrivance," a "stuffed sausage of a puppet" (178), or an "experimental contrivance" (192). Hector Bogus asserts that life is artificial (183) and creates artificial animations (181–183). The scattered pieces of Jezebel in the Cannes animation are revealed to be artificial (137).
Attribute
An object held or associated with a figure, signifying identity or power. Polder Dossman holds a camel goad as an attribute before moving the mountain (205). Polder Dossman's surviving hand holds a camel's flem as an attribute after death (213).
Aura
The electrical shell surrounding a person, translatable into light and color (7). Pilger Tisman's aura is described as dazzling, containing a hundred nonchromatic colors, grays, silvers, brasses, pulsating pallidness, shinings, shimmers, writhing blackness, and areas of light that cannot be fractured (7). It is dimmed but not extinguished during his execution (4), goes out upon death (9), but then reappears dazzlingly at a distance before flicking out of the world (9).
Beggar-King
An oceanic companion archetype mentioned alongside Huracan and Gyne Peribebleene-ton-Helion (155).
Bi-Location
The condition of existing in multiple places simultaneously. Pilgrim Dusmano discusses the problem of bilocation regarding alternate worlds (16). The floor of his main business terminal is believed by some to smell of it (33). Its "kickback" is suggested as a cause for the shimmering effect at the commodity arrival area (42).
Bottoming-Earth
A descriptive term for Prime World, evoking its foundational nature and connection to muck and bottomless sloughs (21).
Branch-Worlds
An alternative term used by "fringies and nonsuches" for the interconnected alternate worlds occupying the same local space (14).
Bridge, Invisible
A high, potent structure exerting a "powerful charm," envisioned by the Pym family as their means of crossing to another world or aspect, facilitated by Pilgrim Dusmano's ritual (53).
Buckling, Parallel Worlds
Described as a "wide tangle" from which Pilgrim Dusmano habitually derived or found advantage (32).
Bundle of Sticks
Pilgrim Dusmano's self-metaphor, representing his existence as a composite of a "million long and skinny sticks bundled together," each stick being a parallel self, none individually constituting a large part of the whole (77).
Call-Tone
An audible signature, a nonchromatic aspect of the body corona, unique to an individual (4, 6). Pilger Tisman's is rough, rambunctious, complex, and powerful, hardly needing amplification (6). Jude Ravel (Doctor) considers it a "signature" but not a complete résumé of the man (6). The brigadier demands to hear it extinguished simultaneously with Pilger Tisman's life (6). It is the last thing to potentially "jump" forward after death, and its reappearance outside the body, possibly seeming to mock, signifies a successful escape (7). Pilger Tisman's tone sounds again triumphantly and mockingly after his death, even taking up the tune "Heads Will Roll" (9, 10).
Carrying-Forward
The act by which certain tricky individuals, particularly cult figures, take something (often memory, identity, or consciousness) with them upon dying (2, 3). This substance is weighable (3, 10). The process involves individual tricks, cataloged by death-monitors (3), and often leaves a "compensating thing" or "residue" behind (3, 10). Tisman succeeds in this (10).
Catch, The
The potential negative consequence or drawback inherent in Pilgrim Dusmano's promise of endless world-jumping; Mary Morey persistently demands he name it (18). Dusmano acknowledges an "extremely improbable failure," a "narrow foul chance" linked to Prime World (18, 19, 20), but initially refuses to elaborate (19).
Cerebral Juglans
A small nodule in the brain, the "remembering acorn," containing compressed memory essences (5). It is a composite of chemical fixes and electrical charges in patterned wrinkles (5). Wilcove Funk (Doctor) monitors and "mars" Pilger Tisman's juglans during the death-weighing (5). Though initially intact after Pilger Tisman's death, its "fat content" (memory, identity, consciousness) is stolen shortly after, collapsing the structure (9).
Cloud-Capper
Og Scath uses this term, likely referring to the Hand from Heaven (190).
Color
A quality potentially absent or illusory in certain worlds (162). Pilger Tisman's aura contains a hundred "nonchromatic colors" (7). The paintings of van Gregory Ghi are suffused with an unworldly, ghostly orange color (66). Colors in the Daylight Museum must be "chaste" and viewable without inducing fever or high unease (59). Polder finds the sharp-lined world lacks the true quality of color, specifically red (162).
Compensating Thing
A new item or residue seemingly left behind by those who succeed in "carrying-forward" something from death (3). Cult figures often leave a "fast-spreading residue" (3). Pilger Tisman is presumed to have left one, which Wilcove Funk (Doctor) likely steals and suppresses (10).
Consciousness
Considered, along with memory and identity, as one of the weighable things that can be "carried forward" after death (3, 10). It is often taken by unconscious persons making the leap (3). Pilger Tisman takes the "container for his consciousness" with him (10). Hector Bogus devises an artificial consciousness for his tortured animations based on an "ingenious resonating circuit" (182).
Container for Consciousness
One of the weighable things, along with memory and identity, that Pilger Tisman successfully takes with him when he world-jumps (10).
Continuity of Memories
Requires attention during the act of dying to ensure successful world-jumping (17).
Corona Spectrum
An aspect of a person that can be measured or observed; Pilger Tisman's is dimmed but not extinguished during his execution (4).
Corporate Good
The justification or outcome Pilgrim Dusmano envisions for consolidating Cyrus Evenhand's fortunes with his own, suggesting it will nourish his parallel selves (89).
Correspondence-Integers
Parallel aspects or representations of individuals existing on corresponding orbs (30). Shaping younglings on one orb shapes these integers elsewhere according to "distance in attitude and space and time" (30).
Corresponding Orbs
Parallel worlds where correspondence-integers exist (30).
Corresponding Persons
Pilgrim Dusmano's term for his parallel selves on other worlds or orbs; he believes he is well-organized regarding them and that the different "integers" of him aid one another (30).
Counterworlds
Horrendous ghost worlds erected by tricky departing cult figures that impinge upon the real world, causing dislocation, disturbance, erosion, and fright (4). Pilgrim Dusmano claims to speak of these "with no first world" (117).
Dark Contingency
Pilgrim Dusmano's term for the possibility of Prime World's existence and the associated dangers (21).
Darkness
Associated with Prime World (21) and the private state imposed on the watchers in the Narrow Corner by the pan-morph's vision (122). The Media Lords are identified by Noah Zontik as the true Lords of Unreason and Darkness (107). Frosty breath of unseen spirits is visible against the darkness in the Narrow Corner (125).
Dazzle
A quality attributed to Pilger Tisman, whose aura makes him "a dazzle!" (7). Also part of the "shimmer" associated with Pilgrim Dusmano (37, 115, 203), and his "dripping hands" (115). Pilgrim Dusmano cannot become such a dazzle if he is merely derivative swamp gas (23).
Delirium (Total)
The state of mind prevalent on Prime World, characterized by absolute logic that permits no deviation; considered the most fearful thing anywhere (21). Those on Prime World have "delirious minds" (22).
Delta Pattern
A brain impulse pattern of about three counts per second emitted by Pilger Tisman during his death throes, considered unusual for an unconscious person or a world-jumper, indicating a personal trick for gauging his jump (8).
Devil
The curator identifies the force driving the destruction of the Consul as the "tragos-goat himself. . . the devil" (68).
Devil-Angels, Archetypical
The "unstable-hundred company" which Palgrave Tacoman joins upon the universal acceptance of his testament (154).
Devil-Revel
Pilgrim Dusmano's term for the collective, murderous pleasure derived by a nation from the destruction of a Consul (66).
Devils
A group whose personal testaments constitute the "ocean" of the group unconscious or mass media (143). They are distinguished by literary/eidetic styles and assigned identifiers (letters, Tarshish Syllabary signs, elemental symbols) (143). There are believed to be as many such publishing devils as there are elements (143). Nine new media devils have been discovered concurrently with nine new elements (143). They also possess the power to seize and dismember an unmasked man (70).
Dice Throwers, High Seven
An elite group associated with Fate, also called the "High Seven" (197, 198) or simply "High Dicers" (200). Their dicing is another name for Fate (201). Membership confers the highest status (197). A vacancy exists due to Merope's disappearance, and there is speculation Polder might fill it (197). Moira Morey declares it must be believed Polder is one of them (198).
Dimwits
The original people of the Prime World, described as giants who are the "pride of prime" (24).
Dingy Moment
The duration Og Scath will spend following Polder into the "shallow and dingy ditch" instead of Hell (213).
Dunlunk's Fifth Law
“Any action in any world will inevitably set up parallel actions in parallel worlds” (30). Pilgrim systematically applies this law in his teaching and manipulation of selected minds; his worlds are not isolated from the consequences of one another.
Ecumens
Alternate term for inhabited worlds or planes of existence; Pilgrim Dusmano seldom enters new lives, earths, or ecumens unprepared (30).
Eidetic Life
A state of existence, possibly created by Media, which Hector Bogus contrasts with "real life" but suggests can still exist (192).
Eidetic Lords
Powerful entities associated with the Media Lords (175, 181) and possibly involved in the creation or manipulation of beings like Polder Dossman (175). They are served by individuals like Hector Bogus (181, 185) and potentially represent forces of unreason and darkness (175). Polder refers to Hector Bogus as an Eidetic Lord (185). They seem to possess or control specific types of power or reality (181, 186).
Eidolon Fiber
A non-flesh component identified in the analysis of Polder Dossman's body, mixed with human and regressed flesh (212).
Eidolon(s)
