Noah Zontik, divinely commissioned to protect Pilgrim Dusmano (27), acts as "the Umbrella" (28) but struggles with his charge's evil and his own compulsive loyalty, and he follows Pilgrim into death (84, 104, 119–120). Og Scath mirrors this role for Polder Dossman, identifying himself as the primordial ﬁgure holding the umbrella over the Ark (172, 177), tasked with protecting Polder (168) despite personal reluctance (174, 207). He fails to prevent Polder's fatal challenge (204) and dies almost concurrently (214). The Hand of Heaven, a contracted meteorological protection for Polder (168), is subverted by Hector Bogus to kill him (190–191) and is later destroyed by Polder's own actions (206–207).
Proto-Protein
A commodity sourced from Supply, subject to quality checks (e.g., being too agglutinative or too loose) (36).
Provinces, The
The place of origin of the mock Lord Spiritual, Trenchant, suggesting he is an outsider or less sophisticated than the established Lords (78).
Pseudos / Pseudoscientists
Groups who, along with "fringies and nonsuches," correctly believed alternate worlds occupy the same local space (14).
Psyches
Mentalities or individualities, particularly those of the young, which Pilgrim Dusmano finds exquisite pleasure in moulding, eradicating, forcing, or raping (31).
Public Opinion
Had cried out for Pilger Tisman's death (2). Pilgrim believes mountains can be moved if compelling public opinion is first generated (187).
Purblind
The state of near-blindness induced in the watchers above (Knacker, Wut, Pym child) when the pan-morphic Pilgrim establishes his vision as dominant in the Narrow Corner (122).
Purple Pout
A possible, trivial cause of death speculated for the defiant younger Pym child when Pilgrim disposes of its still-warm body (56).
Purpose
The quality attacked by the Media Lords (107). Noah Zontik claims the Media Lords serve no purpose (107). Polder argues the whole purpose of power is to be abused (186). The cerebral juglans' purpose had only lately been discovered (5).
Putty Dwarf
An entity present with Lorica and Albrecht Fairbrow on Oraioi Polloi (148). He argues that all things become "putty" in the hands of those who join the "great creative ocean" (148), dismisses Lorica as common (148), and promotes the value of "antilife" (149).
Puzzler
Polder Dossman's assessment of the young Oak Scath, feeling a sense of prior encounter despite memory gaps (174).
Pym Family (Wife, Elder Child, Younger Child)
Aubrey Pym's wife is initially enthusiastic about transferring (39), the elder child is compliant (53), but the younger child is defiant and preternaturally hostile (40, 53–55). All three are ritually killed by Pilgrim with the stone knife after Aubrey's death, to accompany him as "strings" on his mission to Supply (54–55). Their bodies are disposed of in the grindershredder (56). The younger child reappears as a malevolent entity in the Narrow Corner afterlife (122, 124, 126, 128, 129).
Pym, Aubrey
An employee in Pilgrim Dusmano's commerce division (33). Approaching Pilgrim nervously, he asks for a raise (33–34). Pilgrim designates him as a messenger to Supply, using Pym's wife and two children as "hostages" (34). He is dispatched with his family to Dongola via a ritual involving apprehension, an invisible bridge, and throat-cutting with a stone knife (38–39, 53).
Pyrotechnic Flesh
A quality ascribed to Pilger Tisman and many cult figures, suggesting a spectacular, perhaps explosive or dazzling, nature inherent in their physical being, possibly required for their role (8).
Pyrotechnics
Spectacular displays, easy to achieve in the world (8). The apparent death of Pilger Tisman is called an "end of pyrotechnics" just before his successful jump (9).
Python
One of the forms assumed by the demented Pym child entity in the Narrow Corner as it destroys the ariel (128). Also listed as an archetype residing in Domdaniel, alongside Corn-Mother, FenrisWolf, and Hermaphrodite (154).
Quack World
One of the enumerated aspects defining the nature of the Prime World of prime people, listed alongside the uninfused, grubby, spiritualist, and Fortean worlds (23).
Quasi-Forbidden Area
Describes the shadowy, secretive nature surrounding all dealings with the entity or location known as Supply, contributing to the Commerce leaders' inability to recall details about it week-to-week (35).
Raffels, Judas (Doctor Medical)
One of the eleven cult members present during the final gathering (103). He challenges Lord Fairfronter's interpretation of Pilgrim (106), expresses disbelief in spirits but interest in Pilgrim's mutable medical body and detached shadow (106). He develops a new talent for remote viewing (108, 111), reports on Cyrus Evenhand's death and the shift of the Lords' attention to Pilgrim (108–109). He betrays Pilgrim's hiding place to the militia (114) and whistles "Heads Will Roll" as he leaves with them (114). Along with John Augustine (Doctor), he declares Dusmano dead and receives chits for stipends (118), and later pronounces Mary Morey dead for the same purpose (119). He is then killed by the militia with horses after Noah Zontik (120).
Rampart University
An institution where Pilgrim Dusmano maintains a "seedbed or seminary" to cultivate selected students each morning (29).
Raphaelson, Judah (Doctor)
One of the three outstanding doctors attending the death-weighing of Polder Dossman (210). He questions the nature of Polder's physical composition (212) and notes the finality of Polder's "last jump" (215).
Ravel, Jude (Doctor)
One of the three "outstanding doctors" attending Pilger Tisman's death-weighing (1). He comments on Tisman enduring pain well, discusses animal death rituals (2); Doctor Funk comments on the failure to deliver a showy death. He admires Tisman's complex and powerful call-tone (6) and explains how the tone might signal Tisman's successful escape after death (7). He whistles the tune "Heads Will Roll" after Tisman's successful jump and the brigadier's threats (10). He muses on the erasure of Tisman's brain data after the jump (10–11).
Raw Material
Hector Bogus views Polder Dossman as such, fit for being chopped and harvested (186).
Reals
A term used by Hector Bogus to denote actually existing entities or phenomena, contrasting them with the artificial or eidetic (192).
Recompense
Deemed unreal or an illusion according to Pilgrim Dusmano's philosophy based on the existence of multiple worlds (16).
Red
A quality of color Polder Dossman finds missing in the sharp-lined world, lamenting its absence even in blood (162). Also used to describe the color of tinges in Pilgrim Dusmano's shadows, possibly indicating "raw bloodiness" (61); the "red history" formed by folkknitting (67); the "red murder-rapture" known by Judas (68); the "red flute notes" associated with Pilgrim's shadow (62); the "rich red ritual roast meat" of Blut (87); and the "red brown fire" color of the King Boar (156).
Redacted
How Pilgrim Dusmano believes his clumsy killing of Hut must be "heavily redacted, revised, scripted, dramatized" before entering his cult's gestes (25).
Reflections (of Persons)
In some belief systems about limited souls, three out of four persons are considered not "true persons" but mere reflections (14). Noah Zontik suggests Pilgrim Dusmano is a reflection, not a real person (23).
Regressed Flesh
A type of primordial or devolved flesh, possibly synonymous with "camel flesh" or "humpbacked clay," identified by Vonk (Doctor) as one of the components mixed with human flesh and eidolon fiber in Polder Dossman's body (212).
Remembering Acorn
See Juglans, Cerebral (5).
Rennet
Camel rennet is noted by the Camel Town lad as being highly regarded by housewives, second only to cow-calf's stomach rennet (166).
Residue
A "new and compensating thing," often "fast-spreading," left behind by departing individuals (especially cult figures) who take something with them in death (3). Wilcove Funk (Doctor) potentially steals and suppresses the residue left by Pilger Tisman (10).
Resurrection Blues
A sickness and fatigue experienced by some world-jumpers upon arriving in a new world; suffered by Polder Dossman (159).
Resurrection of Lazarus, The
One of the ten thousand dramas performed on Cannes World, based on a Doré illustration (140). Depicted as always a joy to watch, featuring Lazarus rising putrid and staying thirsty, with the audience participating by keeping a cup of water from him (140). Pelion Tuscamondo orders mountains added to its backdrop (141). It is the context for Pelion's deal with Albert Fineface (141–144).
Resurrection Roses
Mentioned by Moira Morey, possibly as an element contributing to Polder's atmosphere or power (". . .the towering aroma of them—") (193).
Resurrection Thirst
The characteristic, intolerable thirst experienced upon being raised from the dead, exemplified by Lazarus (141) but, according to Hector Bogus, not suffered by reanimated eidetic contrivances (192).
Revenge
A motivation seemingly driving the spirits in the chasms of the Narrow Corner, where "all revenges that survive life will wait to be slaked" (125). Also, the fury-child seeks revenge against Polder for its own murder (160). See also Camel's Revenge, The.
Ritual
Formalized acts structure death, transit, cult membership, and public spectacle. Examples include death-weighing, the Pyms' dispatch, the destruction of the Consul, the golden knacker, cult bread and wine, and the Adonis-like boar hunt. These acts combine symbolic authority with actual suffering (1–2, 46, 53–55, 67–71, 97–101, 112–113, 152–157, 210–215).
Ritual Hounds
Pilgrim Dusmano's term for the collective forces of a nation aroused to hunt down and destroy an unmasked Consul (67).
Ritual Killing
A recurring motif performed with specific methods and significance. Mut performs one on Pilgrim Dusmano, using a ritual knife to bleed him into a five-pint tankard (46), which Pilgrim recognizes as a "ritual killing" that affords him time to prepare for a world-jump (45). Pilgrim later uses a ritual stone knife to dispatch the Pym family as messengers to Supply (53–55). The killing of an unmasked Consul is described by Pilgrim as a necessary "ritual murder" for national renewal (71). Pilgrim Dusmano views the consumption of Blut's flesh as a "rich red ritual roast meat" (87).
Ritual Mask
Elaborate masks worn by Consuls to ensure anonymity while performing their duties (69). Mary Morey notes that Pilgrim Dusmano now wears a ritual mask (with cracked-glass jewel eyepieces) instead of a face (69).
Ritual Stone Knife
A very large stone knife provided, seemingly by workmen, along with stone couches, for the ritual dispatch of the Pym family (53). Pilgrim uses it to cut the throats of Aubrey Pym (53), his wife (54), the elder child (54), and, with difficulty due to the child's struggling, the younger child (55). The knife is removed by workmen after the ritual (56).
Riviere
A necklace or arrangement of jewels. Used to describe the shape formed by the nine stars or worlds of the Nine Lives legacy, resembling a "promontory or cape" (134, 140).
Rock-Shrew Joke (Malodorous)
Pilgrim Dusmano's dismissive term for Noah Zontik's analogy comparing Pilgrim to swamp gas, contrasting it unfavorably with an "upside-down eagle joke" (24).
Rotten Thunder
Lorica's frustrated exclamation while insisting that he has been commanded to make Palgrave a good man, despite Palgrave's evil influence (148).
Rubber Knife
The derogatory nickname used by the genuine younger Lords Spiritual for Trenchant, the false Lord and spy, implying his ineffectiveness or lack of substance (79, 85).
Ruler
The concept is largely rejected in the "post age," requiring any such figure (like the Consul) to be anonymous and masked (105). Revealing the human person behind the ruler leads to destruction (105). Polder Dossman sends commands for all rulers on his operating world to abdicate (198).
Run-Amuck Ones
Hector Bogus's term for figures like Polder Dossman who become troublesome due to uncontrollable power or influence derived from "god-goop" (191).
Rut
The code name for Cyrus Evenhand, the Consul, signifying the rod, scepter, or authority (49, 89, 94). Cyrus Evenhand, under this name, listens in on Pilgrim's conversations (76).
Rutting Season
Occurs in a specific alternate environs recalled by Pilgrim Dusmano, during which young male adults become horned and hoofed for a six-week interlude of intense activity ("Oh, that season!") (17). Pilgrim also promulgates "dynamic rutting as a fine art," contributing to his status as a Lord Spiritual (73).
SALVATORE
The name used by the coroner when addressing the police brigadier during Pilger Tisman's death-weighing ("It never happens that way, Salvatore.") (8).
SATTERFIELD
The public identity associated with Mut, one of Evenhand's henchmen (74). Known for personas like "Strength-inSerenity" and "Strength-in-Purity" (74).
SAVONA
One of the nine worlds or states constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia legacy (134, 146).
SCARF
A small item Pilgrim Dusmano twists in his hands, described as the tool with which he works "small miracles" (21, 23). It can overflow or explode into a mantle or cloak, enabling flight and passage through walls (24), and can be twisted back into a scarf afterward (25).
Scath, Oak
The name used by the young lad Polder Dossman encounters in Camel Town (168). He claims to be ancient Og, who rode the Ark (172, 177), is primordial (176), and was tasked before Polder's arrival with watching over and protecting him, holding the metaphorical umbrella (168, 172). He possesses unusual knowledge (e.g., seeing the writing on brick fragments in Polder's mind) (172), facilitates Polder's business (178), but stubbornly resists promoting Polder's cult, finding it not "serious" or "funny enough" (173, 174). He confirms Polder has achieved archetype status (197), warns him against the mountain-moving challenge (204), but still asserts his role as protector (203). He later attends Polder's death as acting coroner (210), questions the doctors about Polder's composite nature (212), feels Polder's thought about Prime World (213), witnesses the final flutter (214), and dies suddenly as well, possibly accompanying Polder "an instant early" (214). See also Scath, Og.
Scath, Og
The primordial identity claimed by Oak Scath (172, 176, 177). He is Polder Dossman's designated protector (168, 172), acting as his "shield" (203). Possesses "type-memory" regarding Merope's forms (197). Fulfills the role of coroner at Polder's death (210). See also Scath, Oak.
SCATH, OG/OAK
See Scath, Oak and Scath, Og.
SCATTER-LIT
Descriptive term for Pilgrim Dusmano's new, postattack eyes, suggesting fragmented or dispersed light (61).
SCATTER-RAY
One of the forms of Media transmission mentioned by Hector Bogus, categorized alongside focus-ray, ether-tinsel, and solid-light transmission as being exclusively of the "obscenity sort" (184).
SCATTERFIELD PHILOSOPHY
One of the attributes contributing to Pilgrim Dusmano's status as a certified Lord Spiritual (73).
SCENES (OFF-THIS-WORLD / OUT-OF-MIND)
Deep, abiding, reflected images flickering in Noah Zontik's eyes when looking at Pilgrim Dusmano (or in Og Scath's eyes looking at Polder Dossman), depicting events that happened long ago and far away, often to other people (parallel persons) rather than the observers or the observed (32, 175).
SCENT (OF PILGRIM)
Used metaphorically by Randal Muckman to identify Pilgrim Dusmano as the probable source of information ("From a knowledgeable man whose dishonesty few doubt" would have the scent of Pilgrim all over it) (58).
SCHIRM
German word for shield or screen; used by Oak Scath when describing his protective role over Polder ("I must hold the shield over him, the schirm. . .") (168).
SCREAMING METALS
Certain metals used in instruments which, under extreme stress from torsion and heat, respond with complex wave patterns that Polder Dossman perceives as screams of agony (183).
SCRIVENER (DEVIL)
A category of "testifying devil" whose works constitute the collective unconscious or mass media (143). Initially identified by letters ('a,' 'b,' 'c'), later requiring the Tarshish Syllabary and elemental symbols for classification (143). Nine new scrivener or media devils were discovered concurrently with nine new physical elements (143).
SCULPTOR-STATUE
An analogy used by Hector Bogus: an old sculptor carves a statue of a sculptor, putting too much of himself into it; this statue then carves a more sophisticated one, and so on for nine iterations, ending in "rapture-flesh" eidolons who turn on the original sculptor (196).
SEA-CHANGE STATION
A location mentioned by the body-smith in the Narrow Corner; he tells the pan-morph he cannot return there (126).
SECOND-BEST
The defining characteristic of Camel Town and of the camel, according to the local lad Oak Scath; they are reportedly second-best in every possible category but best in none (164).
SEEDBED
Pilgrim Dusmano's term for the seminary of selected students he cultivates at Rampart University (29).
SELF-DESTRUCTION
Advocated by Pilgrim Dusmano as a "strong possibility" and potentially preferable to dying under the "misdirection of others," especially since death is seldom final (17).
SENDING (OF MESSENGERS)
The act of dispatching agents, typically families, to Supply (36). Described as involving a "squeamish," "outre," "grotesque," and ritualistic process requiring a specific frame of mind and shrouded in haziness (36, 40, 53).
SEVEN SISTERS OF THE PLEIADES
Merope, one of the High Seven Dice Throwers, is identified as one of this group (197).
SEVENTY-FIVE OVER SIXTY-TWO
The maximum permissible reading on the "unease index" when viewing art at the Daylight Museum (59).
SHADOW WORLDS
Dimensions encountered when dealing with "obstreperous dying folks" like world-jumpers; Doctor Funk claims he cannot see or touch them but sometimes gets a "small noise" from them in his own tone (11).
SHADOW(S)
Can possess unusual properties. Mary Morey's only shadow is said to be her brother James (60). Pilgrim Dusmano casts multiple, shifting shadows ("Whole parades of shadows") even when still, projecting them from his "breathing body"; these shadows may be the "prime" reality, with the fleshed Pilgrim being derivative (61). The curator notes Pilgrim "exteriorizes badly or unevenly," with "red tinges" in his shadows suggesting involvement in bloodiness (61). Judas Raffels observes that Pilgrim's shadow refuses to follow his body (106).
SHARPIES (JUMPING OFF A WORLD)
In the opening “World-Jumper's Ballad,” sharpies are the clever ones who jump off a world, contrasted with dummies who stay upon it (1).
SHEOL SHUCKINS
A location (perhaps a museum or shop) where one could observe expensive crockery made from swamp-born clay fired in hell (60).
SHIELD
A protective influence or entity. Noah Zontik is designated by God as Pilgrim Dusmano's friend and shield (27) and later refers to his protective sigil, the Iris Umbrella (84). Oak Scath identifies himself as Polder Dossman's shield (168, 203), linking this role to holding the umbrella over the Ark (172). Hecklers possess shields that deflect Polder's lightning (201) and protect against electrical and meteorological attacks (202).
SHIMMER
A dazzling visual effect associated with Pilgrim Dusmano (37, 115), Pelion Tuscamondo (139), and Polder Dossman (203). Also, the quality of the enigmatic floor at Pilgrim's main business terminal (33) and the constant effect enwrapping the commodity arrival area, possibly caused by "Bi-location kickback" (42). Mentioned alongside "shinings" in Tisman's aura (7). Pilgrim is described as one of a multitude of "shimmering persons" needed to direct the Lords of Media (186).
SHINING MOUNTAIN
The specific mountain looming above Camel Town, which the hecklers challenge Polder Dossman to move (205). Polder successfully moves it in a cataclysmic event, after which it stands briefly over the gathering, kills the hecklers with falling boulders, and moves off to the south and east (205).
SHININGS
Visible emanations noted in Pilger Tisman's complex aura, some "cut loose from any color at all" (7).
SHISK-SPEAR
The only utensil provided for Pilgrim Dusmano to eat the roasted flesh-meat (Blut) at the Media Club (87).
SHOCK-PLASTIC YARD
The location where Hector Bogus has Polder Dossman taken to be reanimated by galvanic shock administered via a giant condenser belonging to a shock-plastic manufacturing company (191).
SHOWY DEATH
The kind of death expected from a cult figure, which Pilger Tisman planned but failed to deliver due to the shock and pain of his execution (2).
SIGNATURE
Doctor Jude Ravel's term for Pilger Tisman's unique call-tone or person-tone (6).
SIN
A concept Pilgrim Dusmano claims his followers can commit without remorse (116). Evenhand states his faith commands him to love the sinner but hate the sin, questioning if this applies to a "reticulated mechanism" like Pilgrim (77).
SINEWY HANDS
See GRIPPING HANDS (SINEWY).
SINFULNESS
Noah Zontik tells Pilgrim he is likely to lose his life "for your sinfulness" (84). Pilgrim retorts that sinfulness is the "aim of life, the culmination," asking if Noah doesn't understand that a truly successful life must be fulfilling in its sinfulness (84).
SINGLE SKIN
The state the body-smith intends to nail the panmorph into, ending his ability to change form (126, 130).
SKY-PAGEANT
A minor atmospheric display Hector Bogus offers to provide for Polder's cult, contrasted with the major phenomena Polder seeks (195).
SKY-SIGNS AND PRODIGIES
The services advertised on the note attached to the pointing finger of the Hand From Heaven, offered by "Multi-Media Productions" (170).
SKYQUAKE
One of the phenomena accompanying the moving of Shining Mountain (205).
SLATE STRATA
Geological formations rent apart with a "riving wail" during the moving of Shining Mountain (205).
SLEEP BROADCAST, DOCUMENTARY
A technique used by the knacker to incapacitate overseers while illicit cult combinations or transfers are arranged (90).
SLEEP-MAN RECLAIMED FROM THE OCEAN
The literal meaning of the name Polder Dossman (159).
SMART SET
One of the nine worlds or states constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia legacy (134, 146).
SOAP AND OIL EXTRACTORS
The destination for animal carcasses collected by ordinary knackers (88).
SOLACE
One of the qualities said to drip from the "dripping hands" of figures like Pilgrim Dusmano (115) and Polder Dossman (203).
SOLID-LIGHT TRANSMISSION
One form of Media communication mentioned by Hector Bogus, categorized as being exclusively of the "obscenity sort" (184).
SONG OF THE GOLDEN SHOVEL
The source of the epigraph for Chapter 6 ("Eclectic outrage is our rule. . .") (72).
SOUL(S)
Its existence is questioned or debated. Pilger Tisman is said to have had his "soul" escape capture when his memory center was emptied (9, cf. 101). Belief systems differ on soul count: billions per world, or a fixed prime count (approx. 3.5 billion) with others being reflections or "shadow souls" (14). Hector Bogus studies a "soul in hell" via his tortured animation (182). Pilgrim claims that the knacker's soul is trapped forever inside the golden knacker-statue (101). Ravenous, toothclattering spirits in the Narrow Corner eat souls (125). The Pym child seeks the "life and soul" of the climbing polymorph (124). Noah Zontik intends to save the "lives and souls" of both Pilgrim and Evenhand (86).
SOUND-FOSSILS
Doctor Ravel's term for the recorded traces left in the brain, comparing their erasure after a successful world-jump to finding an old record or tape wiped clean (10).
SOUTHGATE COMPLEX
Location of the "hell" museum/experience where one can encounter "hot and dizzy and nauseous stuff" (59).
SPECTACLES
Grand displays demanded by Moira Mara for Polder Dossman's cult, along with prodigies, monstrals, and miraculi (195). Also refers to the proxy death spectacle provided by Longram (211).
SPIRIT(S)
An aspect of being. Judas Raffels professes disbelief in any spirit, focusing instead on Pilgrim's medical body (106). The ariel is said to have had her flight, balance, and spirit destroyed by the Pym child entity (129). Invisible, tooth-clattering spirits with frosty breath inhabit the chasms of the Narrow Corner, ravening to eat souls (125). The "spirit moves" is invoked by Lorica regarding creative opportunity (148). Polder Dossman feels the bottom fall out of his spirits after the mountain-moving (206).
SPIRITUALIST WORLD
One of the aspects defining the Prime World of prime people, according to Noah Zontik (23).
SPLEENS, SPASTIC
Along with deviled brains and goatish gonads, metaphorical organs representing the reactive state of the populace under the influence of "instant agitators" (68).
SPOTLESS
The certified goodness required of a Consul. Evenhand is spotless; Mut says his faults are externalized in his henchmen. Pilgrim calls the curator a spotless sheep and declares his hatred of unspotted flesh. The hatred belongs to Pilgrim, not the curator (49, 51, 66–71).
SPOTS
Flaws or negative traits; Mut explains to Evenhand that his (Evenhand's) spots are "externalized and localized" in his eight henchmen, particularly Mut (51).
SPRINGTIME
The season preferred by Pilgrim Dusmano for visiting the environs where males are horned and hoofed (17). Also the season when Polder Dossman's commercial ventures shoot up like cockleburs (173).
SPURGEON
An associate and employee heading Pilgrim Dusmano's Commerce division (35). He nervously brings up the recurring, forgotten issue of needing adjustments from Supply (35). He reveals he arrived at his position less than a year prior as an "outre messenger" from Supply, though he forgot the details (36). He oversees the drawing up of the "bill of particulars" for the messenger (37, 51). Later present at the final cult gathering (103) and asks why Pilgrim should hide (111). He follows the militia out with Raffels, Zontik, and the Moreys (116).
SQUEAMISH
Spurgeon's assessment of the method Pilgrim Dusmano uses to dispatch messengers to Supply (36).
STALACTITES, SMOKY
Formations lining the passageway to the Narrow Corner, seeming to rhyme verses with limestone and brimstone tone (124).
STALAGMITES, ICE
Not present in the burning chasms of the Narrow Corner, replaced instead by "burning bushes of incandescent iron" (126).
STARS (AS WORLDS)
The Nine Lives legacy is depicted as nine "blue-bright stars" forming a rivière, each illuminated by its own transcendent planet (133–134).
STARS (SEEN AT DEATH)
Pilgrim Dusmano sees stars, jewels, and pinwheels when struck down by Mut; these bright things then lodge in his eyes, creating his "jeweled eyes" (60).
STATUE
Pilgrim Dusmano states his intention to make himself look like a statue, but not a statuette (63). Refers also to the HOLY KNACKER statue (100, 101) and the sequence of SCULPTORSTATUES (196).
STATUETTE (WOODEN)
A small carving by Groben, displayed at the Daylight Museum (63). Though not well-carved, it possesses live monkey/kobold eyes (63), which Mary Morey recognizes as Pilgrim's former eyes, noting the statuette resembles Pilgrim (63). Pilgrim orders it drowned (63), and James Morey holds it underwater until its eyes die and its limbs deform (64, 71). It screams underwater during the process (69).
STEALING HOLES (OR TUNNELS)
Doctor Funk's metaphor for taking away the fundamental patterns of memory from the cerebral juglans; considered impossible, yet "often done nowadays" (6).
STICKS (BUNDLE OF)
Pilgrim Dusmano's metaphor for his composite self, comprising a million parallel persons (sticks) bundled together, none individually significant (77).
STIPENDS
Payments received by doctors for pronouncing persons dead (117). Doctors Augustine and Raffels anticipate collecting several (117), receive chits for them after declaring Dusmano dead (118) and Mary Morey dead (119). Doctor Augustine collects his, including Raffels' death stipend, before departing via private conveyance (120).
STONE COUCHES
Four long benches brought by workmen for the Pym family to lie on during the ritual dispatch to Supply (52, 53). Removed after the ritual (56).
STONE KNIFE, RITUAL
See KNIFE, RITUAL STONE.
STOOL
Referenced in the "Song of the Golden Shovel" epigraph ("And pass huge camels to the stool") (72). Also used metaphorically by Raffels regarding the Media Lords straining to find fault with Pilgrim ("Oh, how all the great Lords are straining at the stool!") (108).
STRAIGHT CORNED MUTTON
Pilgrim Dusmano's dismissive description of the curator of the Daylight Museum, implying naive literal-mindedness (68).
STRAITENED FORM
The final, fixed state the body-smith intends to impose on the pan-morph (126).
STRANGE IMPULSE
See IMPULSE, STRANGE.
STRINGS (ON MESSENGER)
Pilgrim Dusmano activates the family members of a messenger to act as metaphorical strings, ensuring the messenger's compliance or return (36).
STRUCTURE-STOCK
Building material received from Supply, subject to quality checks (e.g., being too magnetic or not magnetic enough) (36).
STUBBORNNESS
Identified by Polder Dossman as the defining negative trait of Og Scath and the world he inhabits, specifically regarding resistance to Polder's cult (174). Polder states stubbornness can be cured via "strategic destructions" (174).
STUDENTS
Young people cultivated by Pilgrim Dusmano at Rampart University (29), including Mary Morey, James Morey, Rhinestone Suderman, and Howard Praise (19, 103). They become disciples and cult members (103). A "bright young student" provides Pilgrim with a theory about the commodity arrival floor (41–42).
STYLI
Writing implements placed in fingers by the creator figure (Lord of the Worlds), enabling written communication (107).
SUBLIMATE, CORROSIVE
A substance kept in a vat by a processor in an industrial yard; Hector Bogus dips the suffering animation (183) and later Polder Dossman (190) into it to kill them.
SUBSCRIPT, CLOUDY
The text accompanying the invisible Hand from Heaven ('Protect this least of mine.'), specifically intended for the protector Og Scath (168).
Suderman, Rhinestone
A large, fair-haired female student of Pilgrim Dusmano (18). Although claiming not to understand or be attracted to him, she acknowledges his correctness (18) and initiates the formation of the Pilgrim Dusmano cult, suggesting "chaos" as its organizing principle (19). She is present at the final cult gathering (103), mourns Pilgrim's departure (104), and questions Judas Raffels (Doctor) about his new psychic abilities (108).
SUGGS
Proprietor of a local dental supply and plug house, whose name is stamped on the bogus-gold plug used by Polder Dossman (200).
SULPHUR
An element in the "handy-fuel" from Supply; its level (too high or too low) is a quality control concern (36).
SUNDOG
Noah Zontik compares Pilgrim Dusmano's dazzling, derivative nature to a shimmering sundog, implying it is merely reflected light (23).
SUPPLY
A mysterious entity, location, or dimension that provides vast quantities of commodities to Pilgrim Dusmano's business (35, 36). Contact requires sending specific messengers (agents) weekly (35–37). The process is difficult and requires secrecy (35, 52). Adjustments to the flow or quality of materials from Supply are a recurring issue (35, 36, 52).
SWAMP GAS
Noah Zontik's dismissive analogy for Pilgrim Dusmano, suggesting that he is ionized, luminescent gas, a projection of the "most dismal swamp" and not a substantial being (23).
SWORD (OF WITS)
Polder Dossman intends to use this metaphorical weapon to open the "oyster world" he has arrived in (159).
SYCAMORE ROAD
A rustic road, deep in fallen leaves and closed to vehicles, down which the cult members walk during the final sequence of events (107).
SYLLABARY, TARSHISH
An extensive script system adopted for classifying "testifying devils" when the conventional alphabet proved insufficient (143).
Tacoman, Palgrave
An identity of the main character, seemingly during his time on the Nine World of Oraioi Polloi (146). He is attended by Jeanie and Albrecht Fairbrow (147), interacts with Lorica (147–149) and the Putty Dwarf (148–149), orders the summoning of mountains for a backdrop (141), and becomes recognized as an archetype associated with a new unstable element and the camel totem (154). He participates in a ritual boar hunt (152), witnesses Albrecht Fairbrow's death (155), confronts the King Boar (156), and experiences a ritual death mirroring the scene on the post boy's horn, becoming a "very good Adonis" (157). His associate aspects continue pleasuring themselves across the Nine Worlds after this death (157).
Tajiman, Paladin
One of the names listed as part of the Tisman/Dusmano/Tuscamondo/Tacoman/Tasman/Thasomen/Theissmand/Dosmens/Dorsetmoon/Dusselmon/Dossman complex (146).
Talismans
Items listed among the diverse goods arriving inexplicably at Pilgrim Dusmano's commodity arrival floor (41).
Talking-Air
One of the groups of Lords mentioned by Polder Dossman (186).
Tankard (Five-Pint)
An old, flip-lidded vessel used by the assailant Mut to collect Pilgrim Dusmano's blood during the ritual attack (46). Mut later drinks the five pints of blood from it in one draft (51).
Tarshish Syllabary
An extensive script system employed for classifying the numerous "testifying devils" whose works constitute the collective unconscious, used when the conventional alphabet proved inadequate (143).
Tartarus
The destination into which the demented Pym child threatens to drive the pan-morph after catching him on the narrow edge of the Narrow Corner (126).
Tasman, Polycletus
One of the names listed as part of the Tisman/Dusmano/Tuscamondo/Tacoman/Tasman/Thasomen/Theissmand/Dosmens/Dorsetmoon/Dusselmon/Dossman complex (146).
Technique, Tracing
The method used by death-monitors to identify and catalogue the tricks employed by dying individuals to carry something forward; described as quite new in the location of Tisman's death (3).
Teleportation
Considered as a possible explanation for the arrival of goods at the commodity floor, but seemingly ruled out due to the lack of any apparent receiver or associated energy consumption (42).
Temperance
Pilgrim Dusmano claims, ironically, that he always makes his mistakes "on the side of temperance" (79).
Teras
One of the potential forms (along with ape, troll, man, frog) resembled by the pan-morphous Pilgrim creature upon entering the afterlife (122).
Testaments (of Devils)
The personal creative outputs (literary or eidetic) of a group of "devils" which collectively form the substance of the mass media or group unconscious (143). Most are without excellence, but a few hundred achieve "group-unconscious publication" (143).
Testaments (Personal)
An individual's unique expression or essence. Palgrave Tacoman realizes his "cranky testament," associated with a new unstable element and the boar motif, has become part of the collective unconscious (154). Albert Fineface facilitates Pelion Tuscamondo publishing his "personal flame and image" or "testament" into this same underlying ocean (142, 144).
Thasomen, Palmas
One of the names listed as part of the Tisman/Dusmano/Tuscamondo/Tacoman/Tasman/Theissmand/Dosmens/Dorsetmoon/Dusselmon/Dossman complex (146).
Theissmand, Paulus
One of the names listed as part of the Tisman/Dusmano/Tuscamondo/Tacoman/Tasman/Thasomen/Dosmens/Dorsetmoon/Dusselmon/Dossman complex (146).
Theleme
One of the nine worlds or states constituting the Nine Lives to La Spezia legacy (134, 146).
Thieves' Honor
Described by the knacker as having become a "patchy thing" in the postanarchic world (97).
Thing Itself, The Larger
An ultimate reality discovered and intimately known on Hector Bogus's world, rendering lesser realities ("ten-times-removed shadows") undesirable (186).
Thing Taken / Thing Left
The concept that individuals who carry something forward ("Thing Taken") from death also leave a "new and compensating thing" ("Thing Left") behind (3). These two may be halves of a unity (3). Wilcove Funk (Doctor) is suspected of stealing the "Thing Left" by Pilger Tisman (10).
Thirst
A significant motif, especially in the afterlife or states adjacent to it. Lazarus experiences authentic thirst upon resurrection (140, 141), an element central to the drama (140, 142). Polder Dossman suffers terrible "resurrection thirst" after being reanimated (192), contrasting with Hector Bogus's assertion that eidetic contrivances do not (192). Polder also experiences horrible thirst upon awakening on the ragged hillside after his jump (159).
Thorn Thicket
A large thicket along the parkway where Pilgrim Dusmano hides after fleeing the Media Club (111). Judas Raffels claims it is "green-thorn time" there despite the season (112). Dusmano emerges from it like a startled stoat upon the militia's arrival (115). Mary Morey predicts Pilgrim will be torn apart there (112).
Thrones and Powers!
Og Scath's exclamation upon witnessing the Hand from Heaven deposit the dead Polder Dossman in an ash-box (190).
Thunder
Associated with the Hand from Heaven (Polder desires the echo and memory of it) (184) and the moving of Shining Mountain (accompanied by unnatural lightning) (205). Also produced metaphorically by Polder's voice (171) and the charge of the King Boar ("royal swinish thunder") (156). The body-smith emits an "apish voice like high-pitched thunder" in the Narrow Corner (126).
Tin Tongue
Derisive chant directed at Polder Dossman by hecklers ("Tin tongue, tin tongue. Empty barrel, broken bung"), contradicting his reputation as the "golden tongue" (201).
Tinsel Lords
Communicators associated with the Media Club and the permanent revolution against the people. Trenchant names them among the groups unable to find a fault in Consul Evenhand (73–81).
Tisman, Pilger
The cult figure executed with Yperite at the opening of the novel. Doctors Funk, Austin, and Ravel monitor his death, but he carries away memory and identity. His person-tone sounds triumphantly after bodily death, and Funk conceals something left behind by the departure (1–12).
Tityrus
One of the potential forms (along with ape, teras, troll, man, frog) resembled by the pan-morphous Pilgrim creature upon entering the afterlife (122).
Token
Something potentially left behind by a successful world-jumper like Pilger Tisman, possibly hidden (11). Also refers to the leather and hair badge of "the Camel's Revenge" found embedded in the spy Trenchant's neck (85).
Token Lust / Token Murder
Pilgrim Dusmano's terms for the ritual drowning of the wooden statuette, viewing it as a symbolic act or "sauce" for the larger destruction of the Consul (67, 71).
Tone
See Call-Tone / Person-Tone / Man-Tone.
Tongs
Used by Mary Morey to ritually place particled walnut bread on the tongues of cult members (112).
Tongue
Used literally and metaphorically. The Marshal of Animations' tongue is swollen and protruding, then pricked by Albert Fineface (138). Polder Dossman is renowned for his eloquent "golden tongue" (171, 201), contrasted with the hecklers' insult "tin tongue" (201). The gift of tongues is flaunted by Polder but dismissed by hecklers as fakery (203). The Lord of the Worlds put tongues in human heads to talk with (107). Obscenity loosens tongues (184). Pilgrim/Polder's tongue feels like clay (118). Tongues are torn out during a Greek Katastrophy (71). Twelve tongues floating in a bowl is a gruesome image invoked by the militia commander (114).
Tonics
Items listed among the diverse goods arriving inexplicably at Pilgrim Dusmano's commodity arrival floor (41).
Topology (of the Other Sides)
The nature and structure of the afterlife realms encountered by world-jumpers; described by Wilcove Funk (Doctor) as varied ("They are legion") and complex, involving different terrains like bluffs, shoal water, and immense heights (9).
Torture
Inflicted deliberately or as part of a process. Hector Bogus tortures small animations in a cabinet (182) and acknowledges Polder's final moments involve intense agony (214). The destruction of a Consul involves torture (67), as does a Greek Katastrophy where the entire community participates (70). The knacker gasps in torture while being killed (97). Longram is given torture gas as part of Polder's proxy death (211).
Torture Cabinet
Hector Bogus's device for inflicting eternal pain on small animations (182).
Toss-Like-A-Bull-Man Reclaimed From the Ocean
An alternative, less preferred meaning of the name Polder Dossman (159).
Touch (Bad-Death)
An ability possessed by knackers; the failing knacker implies that if Pilgrim had touched him during the murder, Pilgrim would have been "spooked" (98).
Tower (Crashing)
The simile used to describe the fall of the combined construct of impaled boar, horse, and rider (Lorica) during the hunt on Oraioi Polloi (153).
Town
Several are mentioned: Camel Town (163); Dongola (39); the small town at the base of the hill in the sharp-lined world (162); the small town near Jerusalem where Lazarus might have been resurrected (141).
Toy
Hector Bogus dismisses the fluttering Polder-sliver as "no more than a toy" and swears Polder himself was never more than one (214).
Tracing Technique
The method used by death-monitors to catalogue the methods of "carrying-forward"; described as new but having already catalogued over 100 tricks (3).
Tract (Cleansing for)
Pilgrim Dusmano's reply, “Cleansing for the tract, camels,” to Trenchant's charge that he swallows camels while straining at gnats (81).
Trade
Lorica is described as being "in trade," specifically selling worlds and systems (147, 148). Hunting boar is considered a fine pleasure, unless one lives by it "as a trade" (152).
Trading Realms
Interworld commercial spheres; Albert Fineface proposes letting his and Pelion Tuscamondo's realms intersect (142).
Tragedy, Greek
See Greek Tragedy.
Tragos-Goat
The "goat" element in "tragedy," identified by the curator as the evil force behind the Consul's destruction, calling it "the devil" (68).
Trail (of Snail/Slug)
Pilgrim Dusmano's simile for the shining worlds he leaves behind him as he spans realities with his "personal celestial body" (76).
Traitors
Status declared upon Consul Cyrus Evenhand and his eight associates, allowing their property to be denominated derelict (89).
Transcendence
Described by Lorica as a "great thing" currently happening to life, comparable to life originally happening to matter; he urges Palgrave Tacoman to "Be a part of it" (148).
Transcendent Man
One of the popular press designations for Pilgrim Dusmano (37, 115), Pelion Tuscamondo (139), and Polder Dossman (203).
Transcendent Muscles Himself
An apparent public moniker for Satterfield/Mut, synonymous with "Strength-in-Serenity" (74).
Transcript (of Requests)
The document detailing modifications needed from Supply, drawn up by Spurgeon and the commerce board (35). Pilgrim takes it to the Pyms (52).
Transfer
The term used by Pilgrim Dusmano for Aubrey Pym's dispatch to Dongola, described as a "transfer upward" to a world of opportunity (38). Mrs. Pym is initially eager for the transfer (39). Cult transfers are described as intricate (92).
Transfixes
A type of art, possibly unsettling or intense, viewable at the Dismal Den or Implosion House museums (59).
Transformation
The process by which materials might be generated at the commodity arrival floor, theorized to occur "in place there" using ambient elements and force generated by the displacement of coincident worlds (41).
Transistors
Components that burst out of Hector Bogus's small animated creation during a torture session (182).
Transmigration (of Souls/Worlds)
The jumping from death to life in another body or world, a central belief related to the existence of multiple worlds (14). Pilgrim Dusmano refers to it as "metacosmosis" and suggests it can be studied and controlled (16).
Transmission Belt
Metaphor used by Noah Zontik when questioning the source of the Dusmano cult's evil: "Does a transmission belt become evil as it transmits, or is the evil to be found in the power source?" (103).
Transworld Impetus
A quality possessed by "spook-arrivals" from other worlds, like the anticipated alternate Pilgrim, giving them an advantage (95).
Trap
Pilgrim Dusmano plans to lure the "Camel's Revenge" group into a trap where they will kill him, fulfilling his desire to be "done to death by mad Camels" (85).
Tree-Worlds
An alternative term used by "fringies and nonsuches" for the interconnected alternate worlds occupying the same local space, implying a branching structure (14).
Trenchant
A young Lord Spiritual from the Provinces with a "furtive look" and the "heart of a squeamish spy" (79). He challenges Pilgrim Dusmano at the Media Club, questioning his authenticity and the validity of his cult (79, 82). He is called the "Rubber Knife" (79); in the later world, Polder identifies Hector Bogus as his counterpart (184). Trenchant is seized by other Media Lords and killed by Pilgrim (83).
Tri-Mental View
The perspective Pilgrim Dusmano claims is necessary to understand the unity of the three seemingly contradictory beliefs about the multiplicity and locality of worlds (15).
Tricks/Tricky
Associated with world-jumpers and cult figures who successfully carry things forward from death (2, 3, 4). Each jumper uses an individual trick (3). Pilger Tisman is described as tricky (3). The Nine Lives legacy involves "restrictive covenants" forming a "string of jeweled worlds" (132), which Polder calls a trick (117). Noah calls Pilgrim's talk "damned foolish" (85). Pilgrim plans a "clever" trap (85). The knacker claims descent from those knowing a "simple trick" for numinosity (93). The coin flip disappearing is called a "prank" and a "trick" (209). Pilgrim notes that the world-jump involves a "tricky escape" (101).
Triptych (Dotty)
A "breath-flubbing," near-masterpiece artwork displayed at the Daylight Museum, titled Dotty. It depicts a girl clothed (left wing), unclothed (center), and visceral (right wing), signed "Joe Smith" on two panels, with the third possibly by a different hand (65).
Troll, Groll's
One of the potential forms (along with ape, teras, man, frog) resembled by the pan-morphous Pilgrim creature upon entering the afterlife (122).
Trustworthy Man
A necessary qualification for being declared governor or guardian over the derelict property of traitors; Pilgrim Dusmano ironically positions himself as such (89).
Tuscamondo, Pelion
An identity of the main character, apparently during his time on the Nine World of Cannes (139, 146). He is depicted as handsome, with a powerful yet intricate voice, possessing a shimmer or dazzle, and known as the hypnotic, electric, magnetic, or transcendent man with dripping hands (139). He is accompanied by Janie (139), watches multiple dramas (140), orders mountains for a backdrop (141), and makes a deal with Albert Fineface to publish his "personal flame and image" into the collective unconscious (141–144).
Twitching Corpses
The result of Polder Dossman using his powers against hecklers at his large gatherings (200, 201).
Type-Memory
A form of ancestral or collective memory possessed by Og Scath, allowing him to recall Merope's past manifestations as female, hermaphrodite, and male (197).
Umbrella
A recurring symbol of protection. Noah Zontik is known as "the Umbrella" for his protective services (28, 103). Og Scath holds a huge umbrella over the Ark on his coat of arms, representing his fated duty to shield Polder Dossman (168, 172, 177, 207). This protective umbrella is later described by Og as having a hole large enough for a mountain to pass through after Polder accepts the mountain-moving challenge (204). Noah Zontik states Polder will need his umbrella shielding him wherever he goes after death (119). Lorica is repeatedly, and dismissively, referred to as an "umbrella peddler" or "umbrella salesman" (147, 148, 149, 153, 204).
Umbrella Man
A nickname for Noah Zontik, reflecting his protective role (103).
Unctuous Umber-Ella Peddler
A descriptive phrase from the Golden Grimoire epigraph, characterizing the nature of the protector figure, likely Noah Zontik (102).
Under-Minds
The deepest layer of consciousness shared by all beings ("glowworm or giant"), containing the collective unconscious or "Folk Ocean" (142). Pelion Tuscamondo pays a heavy toll to gain access and publish his "flame and image" permanently within these under-minds (144). Archetypal motifs, like Palgrave Tacoman's "humpback-flesh camel motif," become active in the under-minds of even inanimate objects like grass (154).
Underlay
The deep, foundational realm beneath the worlds and minds, described by Albrecht Fairbrow as the source of all power and influence, where the demon Aurelion presides over a cartel creating reality (148).
Universe(s)
The totality of reality, conceived differently by various groups. Scientists speculated about billions of life-supporting worlds scattered through space (13). Pilgrim Dusmano contends the space of countless universes is identical to familiar local space (15). Prime World is deemed the dullest possible world within the universes (21). Questions are raised about the total number of elemental components in the universes (143) and whether an umbrella peddler holds the key to their power (148).
Unstable Element
The designation given to the newly synthesized element corresponding to Palgrave Tacoman, making him an "unstable god of an unstable element" (154). Albert Fineface predicts that should Pelion Tuscamondo achieve status among the highest "media devils," his equivalent identifier would have to be an unstable element, as it's the "only kind left" (143).
Upstream
A direction sometimes chosen by "canny" world-jumpers for their leap out of life, heading towards "cliff-faces there" rather than straight across (8). Pilger Tisman's jump "to upstream cliffs" might have created the illusion of a fifteen-year time gap (12).
Vat
A container used for extreme processes: holding molten gold for plating the eviscerated knacker into a cult statue (91, 100), and holding corrosive sublimate into which the Hand from Heaven dips Polder Dossman to kill him (190).
Veil
The metaphorical barrier behind which the anonymous, masked Consuls make necessary governmental decisions (69).
Vinegar, Tumultuous
Describes the state of Pilger Tisman's body chemistry just before it ceases functioning at his physical death (9).
Virgin
The required state (male or female) of the victim in the classic form of a Greek Katastrophy, necessary for the "pleasure" of the ritual destruction to be sufficiently "rich" (70–71).
Vita-Flow
A substance injected into the dismembered pieces of Jezebel's body in the Cannes World drama to keep them "alive enough to talk" for the purpose of asking riddles (137).
Voice-and-Vision Device
Technology used by two of Cyrus Evenhand's henchmen to be remotely present during meetings (26).
Vonk, Doctor
One of the three outstanding doctors attending the death-weighing of Polder Dossman (210). He possesses a huge head, heavy orbital ridges, a protruding muzzle making a chin impossible, a large back-brain, and great good humor; described as a tremendous man with animal vitality and an expert analyst (211). He comments on Polder's composite nature (human, regressed flesh, eidolon fiber) (212), confirms Og Scath's death (214), and notes the failure of Polder's final "flutter" (215). (Seems identical to Wilcove Funk (Doctor) from Pilger Tisman's death.)
Vortex, Fugaro
A secondary magnetic phenomenon suspected, but not confirmed by instruments, to be operating at the commodity arrival floor (42).
Voxo
A personal communication device used for voice transmission (37). Pilgrim Dusmano uses it to receive an angry call from Noah Zontik regarding Hut's death (37–38). Pilgrim Dusmano uses it to contact the reporter Randal Muckman (57).
Vulgarity, Incredible
A characteristic noted in the set of Pilgrim Dusmano's fat jaw (115), Pelion Tuscamondo's jaw (139), and Polder Dossman's jaw (203), contributing to their distinctive appearance.
Walk-In Bijou
An establishment in New Orleans owned by Melchisedech Duffy, from which unusual art objects (Groben's statuette, van Gregory Ghi's paintings, Alessandro's paintings, the Dotty triptych) are loaned to the Daylight Museum (63, 66). Duffy apparently keeps the best items hidden away (66).
Weighable Substance
The metaphorical or literal "material" (such as memory, identity, or consciousness) that certain tricky individuals manage to carry forward with them when dying (3). The capacity to take such substance is linked to cult figures (3) and successful world-jumpers like Pilger Tisman (10). Its transfer is difficult for death-monitors to prevent (3).
Weighing (a Death)
A novel procedure performed upon the dying Pilger Tisman (1) and later Polder Dossman (210) by attending doctors and officials. Its purpose is not to save life but to observe and measure the death process (1), utilizing "highly sophisticated and wildly ingenious equipment" (1). It involves monitoring aspects like the cerebral juglans (5), aura (4, 7), call-tone (4, 6), and brain waves (9) to potentially capture data about elements carried forward by the deceased (3).
Whitebread, Leslie
An elite figure on Oraioi Polloi who becomes the designated spokesman after Albrecht Fairbrow's death (155). He orders the ariel and dog attendees whipped away from the deceased Palgrave Tacoman (157).
Wiggly-Word Lord
Polder Dossman's angry, dismissive epithet for Hector Bogus, grouping him with Eidetic, Media, and Advocate Lords (185).
Wise-in-Death Animal
A creature possessing a clear, stoic acceptance of death, contrasted by Jude Ravel (Doctor) with the "frustrated-in- death" Pilger Tisman (2). According to Ravel's father, such an animal, having accepted death, would proceed to die even if released from the fatal circumstance (2).
Woolly Camel Book of Nursery Rhymes
The cited source of the epigraph for Chapter 12 ("I'll tell you a story about Mary Morey. . .") (158).
World-Jumper / World-Jumping
The act of transitioning between alternate worlds or realities, often at the moment of death (11, 16). Pilger Tisman is a successful world-jumper (11), utilizing a personal "trick" (8) involving the delta brain pattern (8) to evade capture by the death-monitors' "nets" (7, 11) and take "weighable substance" (memory, identity, consciousness) with him (10). The process allows practiced individuals to select destinations or return to specific life stages (17), though a slow or badly handled death can result in a "bad jump" (113, 118). Polder Dossman makes a successful, though rough, jump resulting in "Resurrection Blues" (159). It is distinct from Pilger Tisman's earlier practice as a "body-jumper" (106). The process is sometimes referred to as transmigration or metacosmosis (16).
World-Jumper's Ballad
The source of epigraphs contemplating mortality and transition, containing the lines "We stand like dummies on a world / Or be like sharpies jumping off it" (1) and describing the "end of jumping" (210).
Worlds (Alternate, Counter-, Ghost, Nine, Prime, Shadow)
Multiple realities existing concurrently. Alternate Worlds may be scattered through space or co-exist locally (13, 14); Pilgrim Dusmano claims billions exist "right here right now" (15) allowing for controllable World-Jumping (16). Counterworlds or Ghost Worlds are "horrendous" realms erected by tricky departing souls that impinge disruptively on the real world (4). Shadow Worlds are indistinct realms associated with dying world-jumpers (11). Prime World is a feared, hypothetical foundational reality characterized by absolute logic, inescapable materiality, and links to Hell (20–22, 206, 208). The Nine Worlds to La Spezia constitute a special afterlife Legacy for the rich, existing outside time and offering extreme pleasure (133, 134, 140, 146, 157). These various conceptualizations often overlap or are debated within the narrative.
Wut
Code name for one of Cyrus Evenhand's eight henchmen, signifying "rage or mania" (49). His substantial fortune (96) is targeted by Pilgrim's knacker in anticipation of his death (89, 94), though the knacker is killed before processing it (96–98). He appears in the Narrow Corner afterlife as an "intelligent, calculating, canny, relentless, unforgetting, unforgiving man" possessed by "rage and mania" (125). He battles the hound (James Morey) fiercely, eventually falling into the abyss after the hound tears out his throat (128–129). His rage terrifies the horses used by the militia, resulting in his being killed by simple garrote instead (120).
Yogurt
Mentioned in a comparison of camel products; yogurt from the khudi-cow is considered best in strength and authority, with camel-milk yogurt being second-best (167).
Yperite
An "old ritual gas," also known as Mustard gas, used in executions designed to inflict death "with discomfort" (2). Pilger Tisman is executed using this method (2).
Zodiac Lord
A high status attainable within the esoteric structures of Polder Dossman's world (197). Polder considers becoming a "double Lord of the Zodiac" representing the reconstituted signs of the camel and the boar (174). Og Scath asserts Polder has become one (197), a status Polder later claims (201, 203). Membership signifies integration into the archetypal patterns underlying reality (197). Hector Bogus questions the validity of Polder's claim (197).
Zontik, Noah
The figure described as Pilgrim Dusmano's "one powerful friend" (20, 27, 86) and associate (20). He holds the titles of both Lord Temporal and Lord Spiritual (84), wears the insignia of the Golden Shovel and the Pilgrim Staff (84), and is known professionally as "the Umbrella" for his services in shielding and protection (28, 103). He is tasked by God with protecting Pilgrim, even into Hell (27), a commission he feels compelled to honor despite his disbelief (84, 104). He frequently challenges Pilgrim's actions and philosophy, accusing him of being a derivative projection (23) and warning him of danger (85, 110). He is also assigned to protect Cyrus Evenhand (86). He belongs to the Dusmano cult (84, 103) but struggles with its implications (84, 103–105). He witnesses Pilgrim's final decline (110) and follows him into death, stating Pilgrim will need his "umbrella" protection wherever he goes (119); he is subsequently killed by the militia with horses (120).

Cosmology

The structure of the novel's worlds

The Three True Theories

Chapter 2 presents three apparently contradictory beliefs about the nature of reality and then declares all of them correct:

Scientific View

Billions of life-supporting worlds scattered throughout space in "apt or green or fortunate spots."

Fringe View

Billions of worlds occupying the same local space, the "tree-worlds or the branch-worlds or the crossroad-worlds," all growing on one tree.

Transmigration View

Only one world with a fixed number of souls (about 3.5 billion), most already embodied, with "three of every four persons" being mere "reflections."

The space of the countless universes—this was Pilgrim's contention—was identical with the familiar local space and was in no way larger than that local space. One space did not contain the other; one space did not go beyond the other; they were of the same measure. A man with a good right arm might throw a stone clear across space, but of course it would be an endless rock that he threw.

A schematic of the novel's worlds. The feared Prime World anchors the cosmological argument, and the Nine Legacy Worlds exist outside time. The arrangement is illustrative; the novel supplies no map.

Select a Legacy World or Prime World for details

The Nature of World-Jumping

World-jumping is the novel's central metaphysical conceit, the ability to escape death by transferring consciousness to a parallel world. At the moment of death the jumper's "person-tone," the audible signature of his identity, passes from one world to another.

Requirements for Jumping

Gateway Death
The jumper must die, preferably by violence. "There were never such mountain-climbers or abyss-leapers as these outlaw world-jumpers in the moments of their gateway deaths."
Frame of Mind
Pilgrim tells his messengers to be apprehensive, nervous, determined, daring, and mentally creative. Panic can disrupt the preparation, but the right frame of mind is not strictly required, since Tisman's painful, apparently mishandled death still permits a jump.
Handholds
The doctors describe Tisman probing for footholds and handholds beyond the chasm. This is the narrative's image for the preparation that precedes his leap; the novel does not explain the mechanism.
Directional Choice
"Jumpers sometimes do not leap straight across. Some of them leap upstream for the cliff-faces there. Some of them jump for the downstream bluffs." The direction affects what kind of world one reaches.

The Commerce Connection

Pilgrim's commerce exploits the slight displacement of coincident worlds. His business and his teaching both depend on crossings between worlds, but the novel does not establish that commercial wealth creates the handholds monitored at Tisman's death.

Failure Modes

Not all deaths lead to successful jumps. The doctors monitoring Tisman's death note: "It’s the sign that a man has been extinguished, or has escaped being extinguished." Failure means true death, in which the person-tone ceases instead of transferring. The brigadier of police threatens: "Stomp on his damned fingers!" The brigadier adds: "Don’t give him a handhold. Don’t give him any hold at all."

The Trap of Prime World

"It would not be possible to world-jump from Prime. Hairy and fetish hands coming out of that earth would grip one about the ankles, and grip with bone-crushing strength." Prime World is the one place from which no jump is possible, and its only exits are oblivion and hell.

The Four Last Things

In Catholic eschatology, the "four last things" are Death, Judgment, Heaven, and Hell, the final realities every soul must face. The novel names them directly: Prime World is "the base and anchor of the four final or eschatological things. Thankfully, there are no final things attached to any of the other worlds."

The protagonist's philosophy is an attempt to escape these finalities. He evades death by jumping worlds and refuses to think about Prime World, the seat of judgment. He offers pleasure-worlds in place of heaven, and by teaching that "punishment and death are only illusions," he believes he has abolished hell.

The Eye of the Needle

The Nine Lives to La Spezia answer Christ's teaching that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter heaven. The Legacy Worlds are the concession the rich obtain in exchange: "The rich would not have accepted it without this. The rich have a special Legacy. . . After they die they are permitted to live nine more lives of pleasure almost hysterical in its immediacy and extent before they go to hell."

The arrangement is stranger than a deferral. The Nine Worlds exist outside time and are never used up, so nine aspects can stay in pleasure while a tenth goes to hell. Polder's final fear is that his present, suffering aspect has no share in that comfort.

The Divine Commission

Noah Zontik/Og Scath acts under a divine commission: "I have a commission from beyond to guard him forever, and to share his destruction if I cannot avert it. I believe that I have this commission from beyond, but I do not believe in any beyond." His obedience without belief suggests that a person who denies God may still be bound by God's arrangements.

Accounts Kept

Prime World is defined by its moral bookkeeping: "They keep accounts on Prime World; ultimate accounts, I mean. They keep crabbed, careful, fetishistic accounts." On this account judgment works as record-keeping, in which every debt is entered and every payment required.

Who thus forgets, in hell or hot: / No drop of blood will be forgot?

The Marshal's Daughter, Chapter 10

The Nature of Hell

The novel presents hell literally. When Polder dies, Hector Bogus places a sliver of his heart in a torture cabinet: "One can study a soul in hell by this device. . . The pain is real to the flutter-piece, and the pain is eternal." The miniature torture is an image of hell as eternal, conscious suffering.

The ending, however, leaves the matter open: "It couldn't, of course, be an actual soul screaming forever in hell. It had to be some sort of imitation. But it was quite a good imitation." The screaming is heard, but the narrator leaves it uncertain whether an "actual soul" is screaming.

The Good Man Problem

Cyrus Evenhand is "accounted a good man," and the novel presents him as virtuous as well as powerful. Longram's influence makes barren land flourish. These figures show goodness having real effects even in worlds ruled by Media Lords and eidolon-masters. Against them, the protagonist's amorality appears as a personal rebellion against a moral order that still holds.

Themes

The novel's major themes and how they develop

Identity & Self

The protagonist's identity and what makes a person "real"

The novel unsettles the idea of a stable identity. The protagonist appears under five principal names, and Chapter 11 lists further names. The novel leaves open whether these are the same person, parallel versions, or different beings. Noah Zontik suggests he is "not merely the projection of one particularly dull person. . . He is the projection of several hundred very bright persons."

His death-weighing reveals a composite nature: human flesh, eidolon fiber, and regressed or camel flesh. Doctor Vonk describes an experimental model made by several experimenters, while also confirming that he had been human somewhere along the way. The evidence weakens his claim to be an authentic original without proving that he was artificial from birth.

The question extends to the other characters. The cult followers may be real people or "mere eidolons of an eidolon, mere graven images of a graven image," and it is unclear whether Mary/Maria and James/Jacob/Jake keep a continuous identity across deaths. The novel treats identity as performance, projection, and collective construction, but it still attaches consequences to persons.

Good, Evil & Amorality

The moral structure of infinite worlds

The protagonist preaches amorality: "Amorality is implicit as a total thing in my claim. . . Recompense cannot be real; debt and guilt are not real; punishment and death are only illusions." He argues that if one can escape any consequence by jumping worlds, morality has no force.

The novel, however, is organized around moral categories. Cyrus Evenhand is repeatedly called "a good man." Longram's goodness makes barren land flourish. The protagonist is described as "an incurable rogue." In the novel, good and evil are real forces.

Prime World supplies the threat of ultimate accounting. The protagonist's rejection of it reads as flight from judgment. His final scream suggests that the flight has failed, even though the status of his last world is never settled.

Media, Cults & Reality

The construction of charismatic authority

The protagonist's power derives from constructed charisma: "shimmer," "dazzle," the "hypnotic man, the electric man, the magnetic man." These qualities are artificial, the products of Media Lords and Eidetic Lords who shape collective perception.

Constructed reality nonetheless has real effects. The cult forms spontaneously: "We’re compelled to. . . . By a compulsion, of course. By a blind compulsion." Followers recognize the artificiality yet cannot resist: "I keep saying there's no way I could ever be attracted to him. And I keep knowing I'm wrong every time I say it."

The Group Unconscious or Folk Ocean underlies minds and creatures, formed from the testaments of eidetic devils. By buying admission among them, the protagonist seeks to place his image in every mind. Prime World represents the feared possibility of a reality that cannot be evaded or reshaped by such transactions.

The Camel Symbolism

"Second-best at everything"

The camel is the novel's central symbol. It appears in the title, in the protagonist's composite flesh, in his totem identity, and in the biblical allusion that opens Chapter 9. The camel is "second-best in everything." It is neither the fastest nor the strongest of beasts, but it adapts and survives where others cannot.

The description fits the protagonist, who is a derivative and a projection and who survives by adaptation. His "humpbacked clay" or "primordial flesh" connects him to the camel at the material level.

The saying about the needle's eye shapes the novel's theology: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven." The Nine Lives to La Spezia are the rich man's way around the saying. The protagonist, who is identified with the camel, finds that world-jumping does not free his present aspect from judgment.

Gnostic Comparisons

The novel permits comparisons with salvation through special knowledge, hostility to material limitation, and counterfeit creation. These are interpretive parallels; its characters and worlds do not form a one-to-one map of a Gnostic system.

Gnostic Concept Parallel in Novel Interpretation
Saving knowledgePilgrim teaches controlled world-jumping (Chapter 2).His promise makes escape depend on technique and knowledge. The ending exposes the limits of that promise.
Material confinementPrime World is imagined as heavy, material, and inescapable (Chapter 2).This is chiefly the world-jumper's hostile description of accountability, not proof that material existence is evil.
Counterfeit creationMedia and Eidolon Lords manufacture images and alter persons (Chapters 10–15).Their creative power coexists with cruelty. The novel questions the moral standing of makers as well as their creations.
AntinomianismPilgrim denies debt, guilt, punishment, and death (Chapter 2).His rejection of moral law is explicit. It should not be treated as a description of every Gnostic tradition.
Image and originalNoah challenges Pilgrim's claim to be a prime person (Chapter 2).The original-copy problem crosses several philosophical and religious traditions; it is not uniquely Gnostic.
TranscendenceLorica offers free participation in transcendence (Chapter 11).Palgrave chooses the expensive infernal cartel instead. The distinction is between transformation and predatory self-extension.

Read in this light, the novel rejects the assumption that escaping a world amounts to salvation, and the last scream discredits the protagonist's account of liberation.

Moral Acts and Responsibility

The following table distinguishes acts, agents, and familiar moral categories. The descriptions summarize the narrative; they are not quotations or an exhaustive theological classification.

Character Category Action Latin Term Theological Explanation

Chronicle of Violence

The novel records its acts of violence in close detail. The following table summarizes the principal violent events:

Section / Event Description Passage and Context

Trenchant's murderThe young Lords mutilate the spy; Pilgrim completes the killing.Chapter 6. Pilgrim tears at the dismembered man and crushes the vital center.
