The spectators' appetite for suffering recalls Augustine's account of Alypius at the gladiatorial games (Confessions VI.8.13): watching the violence draws him into the crowd's excitement.

Timeline

Chronology across worlds and the fifteen-year question

PROLOGUE: THE DEATH OF PILGER TISMAN

Frame Opening
Tisman's Execution

The cult figure Pilger Tisman is executed by the state with "Yperite or Mustard" gas. Doctors monitor his death with equipment designed to prevent him from taking "anything with him" into the next existence.

Characters: Pilger Tisman, Doctors Wilcove Funk, Jon Austin, Jude Ravel; brigadier of police (Salvatore), coroner

The Jump
The "World-Jump"

Tisman evades the death-weighers. After death, his centralized memory deposit (the "cerebral juglans") collapses as "its fat content was removed in electrical charge and chemical fix and pattern." This is recorded as an "absolute physical theft from the body." His aura reappears at a distance, and his "person-tone" sounds, triumphant and mocking.

Residue
The Lingering Residue

Doctor Funk discovers a "new and compensating thing" left by Tisman's departure, a shining residue. He conceals the discovery on impulse, hiding the fact that the residue "overflowed his hand and occupied the world, in a very thin but complete manner." The episode suggests that a world-jump alters the world it leaves behind.

Burial
The Burial

Pilger Tisman's physical body is buried later the same day. The burial is attended by only two mourners, who observe from a distance: Maria del Mar and Jacob del Mar, whose presence anticipates their return, still devoted to him, as Mary and James Morey in his next incarnation.

INTERVAL OF ABOUT FIFTEEN YEARS

PART I: THE RISE OF PILGRIM DUSMANO

Emergence
Dusmano's Lecture

Pilgrim Dusmano, a charismatic university lecturer, explains his philosophy of alternate worlds and controlled death ("world-jumping"). He promises endless lives free of consequence, dismissing the "one bad case" of failure as an infinitesimal risk.

Characters: Pilgrim Dusmano, James Morey, Howard Praise, Rhinestone Suderman, Mary Morey

Location: Rampart University

Genesis
The Cult's Formation

Rhinestone Suderman proposes that she and her fellow students form a cult around the "chaotic" figure of Pilgrim Dusmano, driven by what she terms a "blind compulsion." The proposal founds the Dusmano cult, which becomes Pilgrim's base of power against the established order.

The Catch
The Prime World Explained

Pilgrim discusses Prime World with Noah Zontik in the Prismatic Room. Noah describes it as grubby, spiritualist, quack, and Fortean, yet real. He presses Pilgrim to acknowledge either a prime reality or his own derivative status.

Location: The Prismatic Room of the Personage Club

Declaration
The First Strike

Immediately after his conversation with Zontik, Dusmano flies across town and casually murders one of Cyrus Evenhand's henchmen, Hut. The unprovoked killing is Dusmano's declaration of war against his "one powerful enemy," Cyrus Evenhand.

Retaliation
The Attack on Dusmano

The henchman Mut (Satterfield) ambushes Dusmano in a ritual attack, draining five pints of his blood. The blood loss triggers a physical transformation, giving Dusmano his fractured, "jeweled eyes." Mut's wallet, which Dusmano steals during the attack, contains a notebook revealing the secret identities of Cyrus Evenhand (the Consul) and all his henchmen.

Location: The commodity arrival area

Message
The Pym Family "Message"

Dusmano ritually kills Aubrey Pym and his family to send them as "messengers" to his mysterious "Supply." The younger child defies him: "You can cut my head clear off, but you can't kill me. . . I'll hide in the passages and in the glaciers, and I'll trap you there." One of the child's eyes survives the people-grinder, and the child returns as a vengeful fire-drake in the Narrow Corner.

PART II: THE UNRAVELING

Betrayal
The Consul Unmasked

Using information from Mut's wallet, Dusmano leaks the identity of Consul Evenhand to the reporter Randal Muckman. The news spreads instantly by "tinsel broadcast" and turns the public against Evenhand and his henchmen.

Location: Outside the Daylight Museum

Erasure
The "Micromurder"

Inside the museum, Dusmano encounters a small wooden statuette that possesses his "old eyes." Taking it for a remnant of his original self, he has it ritually "drowned" by James Morey. The act is a symbolic self-erasure, in which Dusmano, a "projection" seeking to become an artificial "idol," destroys a remnant of his former humanity.

Greek Katastrophy
The Fall of the Henchmen

Prompted by media revelations, the public unmasks and violently kills several of Evenhand's associates, including Blut, Flut, and Gut. At the Media Club, Dusmano takes part in a ritual feast, consuming a piece of Blut's roasted flesh: "The burned flesh is pleasant in my mouth."

Location: The Media Club

Theft
The Betrayal of the Knacker

Dusmano conspires with a knacker to seize the fortunes of his nine enemies. Once the plan is set, Dusmano betrays and murders the knacker, encasing his body in molten gold to create the "Holy Knacker" statue. The knacker's dying threat: "I'll prepare a welcome for you in a new place, man."

Location: The All-Effects Hall behind the Golden Grotto

Execution
The Final Hunt and Executions

The Media Lords turn on Dusmano. His location is betrayed by Doctor Raffels. A militia captures Dusmano, Mary Morey, and James Morey and executes them by tearing them apart with horses. They are followed into death by Noah Zontik and Doctor Raffels (by horses), Wut (by garrote), and Doctor Augustine (by "private conveyance").

Location: A knoll above the parkway

PART III: THE AFTERLIFE AND FINAL WORLDS

Transit
The Narrow Corner

In the Narrow Corner, the pan-morphous cult figure and his ariel and hound companions meet the knacker, Wut, and the vengeful Pym child. The companions fall after violent encounters; the cult figure defeats the knacker, takes the name Polder, and then falls himself. His descent is interrupted by the Legacy of Nine Lives.

Location: The Narrow Corner / The Camel's Eye

Nine Lives
The Nine Worlds Interlude

The narrative turns to the timeless Nine Lives to La Spezia. As Pelion Tuscamondo on Cannes World, the protagonist pays to publish his testament in the Group Unconscious. As Palgrave Tacoman on Oraioi Polloi, he pays Aurelion to advance his archetypal status and dies in a ritual boar hunt. These aspects continue forever outside ordinary chronology.

Location: Cannes, Oraioi Polloi, and seven other Legacy Worlds

Arrival
Arrival on the Final World

The protagonist awakens as Polder Dossman on a ragged hillside with two followers, Moira and Jake Mara. He perceives the world as stark, "sharp-lined," and "simple," without depth of color, and its starkness leads him to believe that he may have landed on Prime World.

Location: A hillside near Camel Town

Collapse
The Mountain-Moving

At the height of his cult's power, Polder moves Shining Mountain. The event destroys the Hand from Heaven, kills the main heckler groups, and dissolves his cult through an equal opposing force. Bogus later describes the exertion as an overload that broke the creature. Polder is left convinced that he is trapped on Prime World.

Frame Closing
The Final Death and Damnation

The broken Polder Dossman is subjected to a second execution, attended by officials (Vonk, August, Raphaelson, Og Scath, Hector Bogus) who correspond to those at Tisman's death. This time he does not escape by world-jump. Bogus places a sliver of his heart in a torture cabinet. Three seconds after his recorded end, "he was heard in the very deep distance, far under the queasy feet of all of them." The narrator comments: "It couldn't, of course, be an actual soul screaming forever in hell. It had to be some sort of imitation. But it was quite a good imitation."

The Protagonist's World

Rampart University
Where Pilgrim Dusmano lectures to students, cultivating his "seedbed or seminary of selected students." Many cult members come from here.
The Daylight Museum
Curated by Clarence Music, the Daylight Museum receives artworks from Melchisedech Duffy's Walk-In Bijou. It promises fever and carefully limited unease, measured on scales rather than by visitors' ages. Pilgrim encounters the statuette with his former eyes here.
The Personage Club / Prismatic Room
Where Pilgrim and Noah Zontik discuss Prime World and the nature of derivative persons. An elite establishment with views of the incipient sky.
The Golden Grotto
The public face of the Pilgrim Cult, a place of worship that opens onto the All-Effects Hall. Site of the Holy Knacker's unveiling.
The All-Effects Hall
"Armored and secluded," located behind the Golden Grotto. Contains the furnaces where golden images are cast. Where Mary and James Morey operate the machines and where the knacker processes the henchmen's fortunes.
The Parkway
North of Pilgrim's commodity receiving area, on the edge of town. Contains thorn thickets and a brown-green knoll. Site of Pilgrim's final sermon and execution by horses.
Southgate / Dismal Den / Sheol Shuckins
A "nauseous" complex described as "hell." It is not literal perdition but an unpleasant place where Pilgrim encounters "obscure things that had been in hell literally."
The Mut Body Cult Temple
Temple of the Strength-in-Purity cult, associated with the henchman Mut/Satterfield. Targeted for gold extraction.

The Nine Lives to La Spezia

Cannes World
First of the Legacy Worlds. Site of the Perpetual Animation Festival, with 10,000 dramas a day using live actors. Melodious voices, musical expression, and permitted complaint. Where Pelion Tuscamondo appears.
Oraioi Polloi
The second named Legacy World, whose name suggests the beautiful many. Chapter 11 is set here: Palgrave encounters Lorica, pays Aurelion, and takes part in the fatal boar hunt.
Hy-Brasail
Third named Legacy World. It evokes the elusive phantom island of Irish tradition; the novel does not narrate events there.
Theleme
Seventh Legacy World. Named for Rabelais's Abbey of Thélème, whose only rule was "Do what thou wilt."
La Spezia
The ninth named world of the Legacy, alongside Cannes, Oraioi Polloi, Hy-Brasail, Smart Set, Savona, Delectable, Theleme, and Luogo Perfetto. It is not a last chronological stage: the Nine Lives exist outside time and are never exhausted (133–146, 157).

Metaphysical Locations

Prime World
The original world from which all others derive. "Murk, mud, miasmic fever." Where accounts are kept, metaphors are material, and world-jumping is impossible. Only two exits: oblivion or hell.
The Narrow Corner / Camel's Eye
An afterlife passage point, "sometimes called the Camel's Eye." Built of molten rock (mistaken for ice), shaped by spirits and projections. Where disputes left unsettled in life are resolved. Site of combat between the protagonist's followers and his enemies.
The Group Unconscious / Folk Ocean
The pervading psychic water that connects minds and creatures. Made of the testaments of approximately one hundred eidetic devils. Where Media Lords publish their flames.
Longram's Acres
Barren land ceded to the good man Longram, which flourishes under his influence. "When it had flourished a bit more, it would be taken away from him, and other utterly barren land would be ceded to him." Example of how goodness is exploited.

Media Violence: 1959–1976

Lafferty's novel appeared in 1976, after two decades in which American media depictions of violence changed markedly. The following timeline places the novel's "Lords of the Media" and constructed spectacle in that context:

1959
Pre-Transformation

The Wild One (1953) and Rebel Without a Cause (1955) established rebellious characters, but media violence stayed restrained under strict enforcement of the Hays Code. Westerns like Gunsmoke and Bonanza dominated TV with sanitized conflict.

1960–1963
Hitchcock's Challenge

Psycho (1960) and The Birds (1963) pushed mainstream boundaries. The assassination of President Kennedy (1963) brought real violence into American homes through television.

1964–1967
Code Collapse

The Hays Code declined. Directors such as Peckinpah and Penn tested its limits. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) introduced graphic, realistic shootouts. Television coverage of the Vietnam War brought images of distant conflict into American homes.

1968
The Watershed Year

MPAA ratings (G, M, R, X) replaced the Hays Code and gave filmmakers more latitude. Romero's Night of the Living Dead brought explicit cannibalism and death to the screen.

1969–1972
Aestheticized Brutality

The Wild Bunch (1969) made prominent use of slow-motion, "balletic" gunfights. A Clockwork Orange (1971) stylized "ultraviolence." The Godfather (1972) made graphic Mafia killings central to its story.

1973–1974
Horror's New Register

The Exorcist (1973) brought graphic horror to a mass audience. The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974) helped shape the later slasher genre. Watergate deepened distrust of public authority, while urban unrest exposed political and social conflict.

1975–1976
Publication Context

Jaws (1975) blended suspense with implied violence. Taxi Driver (1976) explored urban violence and vigilantism. Carrie (1976) ended in a telekinetic bloodbath. Lafferty's Not to Mention Camels, in which Noah Zontik calls the Media Lords "the true Lords of Unreason and Darkness," appeared the same year.

Contributing Factors

Technological

Improvements in special effects (blood squibs, prosthetics) enabled realistic violence. Color television made battlefield footage more immediate.

Cultural

The Vietnam War, the civil rights struggle, and political assassinations unsettled American public life, and darker, more violent media reflected those anxieties.

Regulatory

The Hays Code's fall and the MPAA system's rise permitted explicit depictions. An industry rating system replaced the industry's earlier content code; both were forms of self-regulation.

Anticipation

Lafferty's "Media Lords" who "can play any realm or any world like a piano" and "compel a world absolutely to any notion" anticipate concerns about media influence that would intensify in subsequent decades.

Allusions & Sources

Biblical, literary, and mythological references

Jonah and the Novel's Title

Nineveh, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons that know not how to distinguish their right hand from their left, not to mention many camels.

God (Jonah 4:11)

Chapter 3 adapts God's final question to Jonah about Nineveh (Jonah 4:11), replacing the biblical cattle with camels. The title thus joins divine concern for the morally undiscerning city to the protagonist's animal motif. The novel's opening epigraph is instead attributed to Tractatus, Lament of the Times.

The Eye of the Needle

It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven.

Matthew 19:24

The Nine Lives to La Spezia complicate the image of the rich man and the needle's eye. Chapter 9 pairs the saying attributed to Matthew with a comic explanation of how a camel performs the trick. The Narrow Corner, also called the Camel's Eye, makes the passage perilous. The later chapters allow nine aspects to stay in pleasure while another suffers damnation.

Og and the Ark

Noah Zontik/Og Scath claims to be the giant Og, King of Bashan, one of the last of the Rephaim (Numbers 21:33, Deuteronomy 3:11). In Jewish midrashic tradition, Og survived the Flood by clinging to the outside of Noah's Ark. In Lafferty's version, Og held an umbrella over the poorly sealed main hatch, which kept the vessel from sinking and earned him God's commission to protect others ever after.

Og therefore predates the Mosaic covenant. He protects the protagonist even into hell and discharges the duty despite his own disbelief.

Jezebel and Jehu

The Perpetual Animation Festival stages Jehu's Companions Finding the Remains of Jezebel. In 2 Kings 9:30–37, the dogs leave her skull, feet, and palms; the biblical account does not explain this as a matter of taste. Lafferty's staged body parts ask riddles. The Marshal's daughter adds a warning that no drop of blood will be forgotten, unsettling the spectators' pleasure.

Lazarus

On Cannes World, spectators in The Resurrection of Lazarus use their group mind to move a cup of water out of the thirsty man's reach. The cruelty inverts the compassion of the resurrection story in John 11 and also recalls the thirst of the rich man in the separate parable of Lazarus in Luke 16.

The Four Last Things

The Four Last Things are Death, Judgment, Heaven, and Hell. Pilgrim's teaching denies final consequence, while Prime World represents his fear that an ultimate accounting still awaits him. The Legacy Worlds complicate the pattern, since they endure forever but cannot console Polder's isolated tenth aspect at the end.

Real Authors Quoted

Oscar Wilde
Chapter 7 begins with two lines attributed to O. Wilde, followed by an answering couplet from Hound Dog Huckster. Together they connect multiplied lives with multiplied deaths.
Hilaire Belloc
"They order things so damnably in hell." Opens Chapter 10 and links the apparent paradise of the Legacy Worlds to hell. The line is typical of Belloc's mordant Catholic verse.
F. Scott Fitzgerald
Chapter 10 attributes the abbreviated observation “The rich are different from us” to Fitzgerald. It recalls The Rich Boy, whose narrator describes the very rich as different from “you and me.” Lafferty extends that difference into the privilege of the Nine Lives.
Gustave Doré
The French artist and engraver (1832–1883) whose works provide the basis for "Doré Day" at the Perpetual Animation Festival, with 10,000 dramas based on his illustrations. His Gothic, dramatic style fits the festival's excess.

Chapter Epigraphs (Fictional Sources)

Lafferty invents texts and authors for many of his chapter epigraphs:

"World-Jumper's Ballad"
Appears in Chapters 1 and 15, framing the novel with a contrast between the choice to jump off a world and the eventual end of jumping.
Arpad Arutinov, The Backdoor of History
"It is difficult to maintain historical calm in recounting them." Introduces the Nine Lives sequence.
Clement Goldbeater, The Enniscorthy Chronicle
Describes the Legacy: "After they die they are permitted to live nine more lives of pleasure almost hysterical in its immediacy and extent before they go to hell." The Enniscorthy reference connects to Lafferty's Enniscorthy cycle.
Hound Dog Huckster
"And when the ritual hounds are done / The dead are you and I." Sardonic verse on mortality and consumption.
Endymeon Ellenbogen, Arena del Mar
Epigraphs on spectacle and entertainment.
Tractatus, Lament of the Times
The epigraph on the making of artificial men, a concern that returns in the doctors' analysis of Polder's body in Chapter 15.

The Nine Worlds' Names

The Legacy Worlds take their names from places, literature, and legend:

Cannes
The French Riviera city, symbol of elite pleasure and film fantasy.
Oraioi Polloi
Greek for "the beautiful many," an ironic play on hoi polloi ("the many," i.e., the common people).
Hy-Brasail
An elusive phantom island of Irish tradition. The name suggests an inaccessible elsewhere; the novel names this Legacy World without depicting it.
Smart Set
The fashionable elite; also the title of H. L. Mencken's literary magazine, The Smart Set.
Delectable
Evokes the Delectable Mountains from Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, from which pilgrims glimpse the Celestial City.
Theleme
Rabelais's Abbey of Thélème from Gargantua, whose only rule was "Fay ce que vouldras" (Do what thou wilt). Later adopted by Aleister Crowley.
Luogo Perfetto
Italian for “perfect place.” It is eighth in the list of timeless Legacy Worlds, not a chronological stage on a journey to hell.
La Spezia
The ninth named world of the Legacy, alongside Cannes, Oraioi Polloi, Hy-Brasail, Smart Set, Savona, Delectable, Theleme, and Luogo Perfetto. It is not a last chronological stage: the Nine Lives exist outside time and are never exhausted (133–146, 157).

Melchisedech Duffy's Walk-In Bijou

A New Orleans art gallery whose wares appear in the Daylight Museum. "Melchisedech puts out trash and keeps the good stuff stored away in a lumber room behind." The biblical Melchizedek was the priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham, a figure of mysterious origin, "without father, without mother, without descent" (Hebrews 7:3). The name suggests hidden sacred treasures behind vulgar commerce.

Giants and Primordial Beings

The Rephaim
Deuteronomy 3:11 describes Og of Bashan as a survivor of the Rephaim. The name also appears in biblical contexts concerning the shades of the dead. These associations suit Og's position across life and death; they do not establish a single certain etymology.
The Nephilim
Genesis 6:4's "giants in the earth," offspring of "sons of God" and "daughters of men." The novel's eidolon-masters and their experimental constructions echo this theme of hybrid beings.
Domdaniel
A legendary undersea palace of evil magicians, appearing in various occult traditions. The novel mentions it as a lodging place for archetypes: "With Corn-Mother, with Fenris-Wolf, with Hermaphrodite, with Python there was a new lodger in Domdaniel."

Celtic & Irish Mythology

Hy-Brasil / Hy-Brasail
Hy-Brasil is an elusive island in Irish tradition, often said to appear only at long intervals. The name fits the novel's elusive elsewhere, although the novel does not describe the Legacy World in detail.
Scáth
Irish for "shadow" or "shelter." Og Scath's name thus means "Og Shadow" or "Og Shelter," the giant who provides protection. (Compare Scáthach, the warrior woman who trained Cú Chulainn.)

Classical & Medieval

Lorica
An adept and powerful man who sells worlds, systems, and galaxies, but is dismissed as an umbrella peddler (147–149). He warns Palgrave against buying archetypal membership in the infernal cartel and offers free participation in transcendence instead. Fairbrow and the Putty Dwarf undermine him. During the boar hunt he kills the first boar after his horse is impaled (152–153).
The Camel Totem
The camel combines biblical resonance with the novel's deliberately comic account of being second-best at everything. The protagonist's totem and regressed flesh connect adaptable animal survival to his own repeated escapes and uncertain claim to originality.
Pelion
Pelion Tuscamondo's given name evokes the Thessalian mountain associated with the giants' piling of mountains against Olympus. The name anticipates Polder's ambition, since Polder does move a mountain, and the feat breaks him.

Archetypes & Eidolons

The novel's "eidolon" terminology draws on Greek eidōlon (image, phantom, apparition). In Homer, eidola are shades of the dead; in Neoplatonism, they are lower reflections of higher realities. The protagonist is partly eidolon, an artificial image rather than a prime reality, yet he produces real effects and real devotion.

The "Group Unconscious" or "Folk Ocean" echoes Jung's collective unconscious, but Lafferty gives it material existence as a literal pervading water made of the "testaments of devils." The hundred or so eidetic archetypes are catalogued "like elements," which suggests a periodic table of demonic influences on human perception.

The Pan-Morph

In the Narrow Corner sequence, a "pan-morph" appears, a composite creature of all shapes that attacks and is attacked. This echoes medieval depictions of demonic aggregates and the classical Proteus (the shape-shifting old man of the sea). The pan-morph represents the formless chaos underlying structured reality, the chaos from which the protagonist, as a "chaotic" figure, claims to derive power.
